title: Decide Eon durability across supervisor, reboot, and machine loss
description:
## Problem

Eon currently has three different durability stories that must not be collapsed into one promise:

- Venus loss is covered: while Orbit remains running, the exact PTY process and authoritative terminal state survive and Venus can reattach.
- Eon supervisor loss is not covered: at Eon f036f798855668b53fa7e099fcb938ba6f0ffe2f, crates/eon/src/main.rs keeps every Orbit process as a std::process::Child and keeps Workspace only in memory. Normal generation stop terminates those children. An abrupt supervisor loss may leave a process and socket behind, but a replacement Eon has no accepted identity, liveness, exit-status, or stop/adoption contract for it.
- Machine restart is explicitly outside EON-C8, EON-C10, EON-C11, and ORB-C1. Arbitrary Unix process state is gone after reboot; a durable record can only reconstruct a replacement unless a separately selected checkpoint or remote-compute substrate owns stronger behavior.

The user-facing term durable therefore needs an explicit failure-domain matrix before choosing a local database, cloud sync, daemon, protocol, or provider.

## Evidence

Repository evidence:

- docs/CONTRACTS.md and README.md state that Eon topology is live-only and machine restart preserves no undeclared process or layout state.
- Eon f036f798855668b53fa7e099fcb938ba6f0ffe2f owns runtime generations, child observation, stop, and in-memory topology.
- Orbit e60554623d2ad1e238fac84d0f8f49be0e81e522 owns the real PTY and sole libghostty state, installs shutdown handlers, and kills/reaps the PTY process group when Orbit exits.
- Venus VEN-C3 already solves transient presentation loss and same-endpoint reconnect. No Venus persistence work is needed for this decision.
- eon-pxn.4 intentionally excluded manager daemons, durable topology storage, PTY handoff, and machine-restart recovery. eon-pxn leaves durable restoration and remote machines separately decidable.

Primary and pinned comparison evidence:

- tmux master 851c5a933d4838c32ad06c248b2ba975d106149c and its official wiki: a background server owns programs; disconnect survival ends if the server is killed or crashes. https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/Getting-Started and https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/FAQ
- zmx 0.7 checkout 4f3739ef98f44d0b639afa57fd76bffcad5d0ef4, shpool 901e18c3ced010073178b78c0ca2a8cdd43e8581, and abduco 8c32909a159aaa9484c82b71f05b7a73321eb491: long-lived session servers own PTYs; per-session servers isolate failure, while shpool delegates daemon lifetime to systemd or launchd.
- Power Failure Resumer 318d24fbab1b5c0ab1242ee19892419b034faa0e: reboot recovery uses durable provider transcripts and resume IDs to discover, preview, explicitly reopen, and verify new processes; it does not resurrect the dead process. https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/power_failure_resumer
- FrankenTerm a19d072439b9ee26f934dd49733c6879abfc8610 reconstructs mux topology and optionally replays best-effort scrollback into new panes. This is recipe restoration, not process survival.
- Atuin 18.17 sync and the current record-store docs: local history is a derived SQLite view over encrypted append-only records; optional end-to-end encrypted sync exchanges records and requires the key on another machine. This is a credible metadata-sync pattern, not a terminal or process checkpoint. https://docs.atuin.sh/18.17/reference/sync/ and https://docs.atuin.sh/main/reference/store/
- Amp Orbs documentation observed 2026-08-12: execution continues on a remote machine, clients reconnect from web or terminal, and setup/resume hooks reconstruct services around an orb. Its continuity comes from moving compute off the laptop, not synchronizing local process memory. https://ampcode.com/manual and https://ampcode.com/manual/orbs
- systemd 40315add9176d2a7c28d8d90490f74e9e982e87b and official loginctl documentation: a user manager can own long-running services and cgroups; lingering can keep it alive after logout and start it at boot. This is a Linux platform mechanism, not a portable Eon product contract. https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/40315add9176d2a7c28d8d90490f74e9e982e87b/man/systemd.service.xml and https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/252/loginctl.html
- CRIU criu-dev f4142635867ebc10b6f72d3ec4911e0dd67cb12c supports Linux PTY checkpointing, but external resources, files, devices, sockets, namespaces, privileges, and version/kernel compatibility can prevent dump or restore. It is not a credible default for arbitrary developer sessions. https://criu.org/What_cannot_be_checkpointed and https://criu.org/Advanced_usage

## Smallest observable decision

Consumer: one local Eon user.

Triggers to classify independently:

1. Venus closes or crashes.
2. the Eon supervisor exits or crashes while the host and Orbit process remain alive.
3. the user logs out or the machine reboots.
4. the machine is unavailable, lost, or destroyed.

For each trigger, decide whether Eon promises exact continued process, explicit reconstruction of a replacement, metadata availability only, or no recovery. Name important failures, one source-of-truth owner, retention and deletion behavior, and whether secrets or terminal content ever enter durable storage.

## Proposed scope

Decision and research only. Compare the options below, select the smallest justified durability tier and sequence, and route any chosen implementation to repository-owned child Beads only after the required EON, ORB, or remote-target contracts are approved.

Out of scope: runtime or contract-index edits; an implementation dependency; a cloud account; an encryption format; protocol compatibility; automatic unknown-process adoption; remote transport; CRIU integration; and claims that replayed text or a restarted command is the original process.
design:
## Options to decide

### Option 0 — keep the current contract

Promise exact continuity only across Venus loss while Orbit and the Eon supervisor remain alive. Improve wording, but persist nothing. This is cheapest and honest, but leaves supervisor crash and reboot as manual recovery.

### Option 1 — phased local durability (recommended product sequence)

1. Same boot: make the session owner independent of transient Eon presentation/control loss, so a replacement Eon can validate and reconnect to the exact still-running Orbit process.
2. Reboot: persist only minimum Eon-owned launch intent and topology needed to preview and explicitly reconstruct replacement Sessions. New Session and process identities must link to, but never impersonate, the prior run.
3. Sync: only after the local schema and deletion model prove useful, optionally encode non-secret records as an Atuin-like encrypted append-only store. Treat terminal frames, raw scrollback, arbitrary environment, credentials, socket paths, PIDs, and process memory as excluded by default.
4. Remote: keep remote execution independent. It earns exact laptop-loss continuity only because the process runs on another machine.

This sequence produces value before a cloud service and keeps stronger claims falsifiable.

### Option 2 — Linux service-manager-first exact same-boot ownership

Run each durable session, or one session host, under the systemd user manager and use stable service identity plus owner-authored status/stop. It reuses a mature native supervisor and can survive logout with explicit linger policy. Costs: Linux/systemd coupling, user-manager and runtime-directory semantics, packaging/policy work, and a required macOS replacement seam. It is a mechanism candidate for the Orbit decision, not the Eon durability contract itself.

### Option 3 — Eon-owned portable session broker

Introduce one long-lived broker that remains the parent and lifecycle authority for Orbit processes while Eon CLI/supervisor and Venus are clients. It gives clean child exit and stop ownership and a portable conceptual seam. Costs: a new daemon/binary, shared failure domain, upgrade and recovery semantics, a second Eon process protocol, and more code than current evidence may justify.

### Option 4 — self-owned per-session Orbit service

Let each Orbit server detach safely from its launcher and expose a narrow authenticated local management identity/status/stop boundary in addition to the one presentation attachment. This isolates session failures and resembles zmx or abduco. Costs: Orbit contract expansion, launch/stdio/signal cleanup, safe identity and stale-socket handling, non-parent exit observation, and Eon reconciliation. Orbit must remain PTY and terminal authority; Eon remains product identity and topology owner.

### Option 5 — checkpoint arbitrary processes with CRIU

Reject for the initial product. It is Linux-specific, privilege and environment sensitive, and cannot guarantee arbitrary external resources. Reconsider only for one controlled workload after reconstruction or remote compute is measurably insufficient.

### Option 6 — Amp-Orbs-like remote execution target

Run the workspace on an existing SSH host or later managed provider, then reconnect clients. This is the only straightforward way to preserve the exact process when the laptop disappears. Do not call encrypted metadata sync remote process continuity.

Record a table with rows for the four failure triggers and columns for exactness, owner, durable data, security boundary, cleanup, Linux/macOS disposition, user action, proof, dependency footprint, and reversal cost. Name the evidence that would justify moving from local reconstruction to encrypted sync or remote compute.

comments.text:
Accepted decision — 2026-08-19 America/Sao_Paulo

The user explicitly approved the recommended selection on 2026-08-19: phased local durability, exact same-boot Eon-supervisor-loss continuity first, and the reduced independently managed per-Session Orbit mechanism selected in `orb-decide-orbit-session-adoption-4hu`. This explicitly reprioritizes the decision ahead of `eon-pxn`; the former planning dependency is no longer a prerequisite to recording the product decision. Closure creates no EON-C, ORB-C, or VEN-C contract and authorizes no implementation.

Accepted failure-domain matrix

1. Venus closes or crashes: exact PTY process and authoritative terminal state continue while Orbit remains alive. Orbit owns the process and terminal state; canonical ORBS owns reattachment; Eon owns product selection. No durable data or new work is needed.
2. Eon supervisor is abruptly lost on the same boot and login: selected first phase. Exact continuation is promised only while the same Orbit remains alive. A replacement Eon must validate the exact live logical Session ID, run ID, component/protocol generation, process-start identity, endpoint identity, and user ownership through the Orbit-authored management handshake before acquiring the sole management lease. Runtime locator data is ephemeral and non-authoritative. The owner-first mechanism is Option D from `orb-decide-orbit-session-adoption-4hu`, without double-fork, a shared broker, systemd requirement, new binary, or new crate unless proof later falsifies that reduced shape.
3. Logout or reboot: the old process does not survive and exact continuation is not promised. The selected second phase is explicit reconstruction of a replacement from a bounded Eon-owned local record. Every replacement receives a fresh run and process identity linked to, but never impersonating, the prior run. Preview and explicit user confirmation precede reconstruction; unsupported launch intent and partial failures remain visible.
4. Machine unavailable, lost, or destroyed: no exact process or local-record availability is promised. Encrypted metadata sync is not selected now. It may be considered only after the local record and deletion model prove useful. Remote execution remains a separate product tier because continuity comes from the process running elsewhere; route it through `eon-az9` rather than presenting sync as process survival.

Distinct outcomes

Exact process continuation, terminal-model reconstruction, topology/launch reconstruction, provider-thread resume, metadata backup, and remote execution remain separate. Ghostty snapshots can recreate terminal-model state but not the PTY process. Provider resume creates new provider/process identities. CRIU remains rejected for arbitrary developer Sessions. Ordinary SSH reaches a live host but does not preserve a process when that host is gone.

Minimum phase-two local record, before any future implementation

- Eon owns one versioned record for the current local workspace: schema version, stable workspace ID, monotonic record revision, clean/unclean marker, bounded topology nodes and selected IDs, and for each Session a stable logical Session ID, prior run linkage, and a typed launch disposition.
- The initial reconstructable launch disposition is the managed default shell/profile only. Arbitrary argv, resolved executable paths, cwd, environment, credentials, provider prompts, socket paths, PIDs, terminal frames, scrollback, graphics, process memory, and raw user content are excluded. Unsupported custom commands are reported as not reconstructable rather than silently persisted or executed.
- Bound the record to 256 Sessions and 1 MiB, with at most one current and one previous valid revision. Write a 0600 temporary file beneath one 0700 UID-owned directory, flush it, atomically rename it, and flush the directory. Reject symlinks, wrong ownership or mode, checksum failure, structural overflow, and newer incompatible schemas. Quarantine corrupt/newer state for diagnosis; never partially apply it.
- The record is retained only for the local workspace and deleted with explicit workspace deletion. A stale revision may be previewed but never automatically replayed. Reconstruction creates fresh run IDs and reports every omitted or failed Session.
- This record is a corruption boundary, not protection against compromise of the local account. A same-user attacker may read or replace it; excluding secrets and arbitrary executable content limits consequence. No cloud/server threat exists while sync is absent.
- Before any sync tier, separately decide end-to-end encryption, key creation/export/loss, authenticated record ordering, rollback/replay detection, accidental-secret review, server compromise, retention, per-device deletion acknowledgement, and deletion tombstones. Key loss means no recovery; server compromise must not reveal plaintext; cross-device deletion must be observable and bounded. No sync contract is implied by this decision.

Ownership and sequencing

Orbit remains the only PTY process, libghostty state, query, presentation, child-exit, and contained-stop owner. Eon remains logical Session/run creation, topology, reconstruction, selection, retention, and recovery-policy owner. Venus remains transient. Any implementation is split owner-first: approve/index the Orbit lifecycle-management contract; implement and prove Orbit; implement Eon consumption against the exact Orbit proof; then run cross-repository acceptance. Phase-two durable-record work is a later Eon-owned contract and Bead, not part of same-boot adoption.

Proof and reversal

The first proof kills Eon with SIGKILL while deterministic useful PTY work continues, starts competing replacements, proves exactly one validates and acquires the same Orbit run, attaches through canonical ORBS to the same PTY child and terminal state, then performs owner-routed ORB-C12 cleanup. It rejects stale/replaced endpoints, wrong IDs/UID/modes, incompatible generations, partial startup, Orbit exit during recovery, and reboot. The phase-two proof later uses a fresh runtime or reboot, previews one valid bounded record, creates fresh identities, reconstructs only supported topology/default shells, and fails closed on corrupt/newer/oversized records and partial launch.

Reverse same-boot work to current behavior if the owner proof cannot preserve exact identity without unsafe PID/path authority. Reconsider systemd/launchd only if logout, start-at-login, or administrator supervision becomes selected. Reconsider a broker only if per-Session Orbit cannot own status and a sole management lease without greater total complexity. Do not proceed to phase two until same-boot dogfood is accepted; do not proceed to sync until the local record demonstrates value without secret capture.

Acceptance disposition: AC1–AC8 are recorded above and in the cited research; AC9 is satisfied by the user approval. No implementation, manifest, package, storage, cloud, protocol, or contract-index change occurred.

title: Set Eon opacity default to 0.80 and roll into Eonova
description:
## Contract

Consumer: local Eon, EonTerm, and override-free Eonova users.

Trigger: a Venus surface is created or reopened without `terminal.background_opacity` in the canonical Eon config.

Result: corrected EON-C13 defaults the existing setting to `0.80`; explicit valid values and all validation remain unchanged. Eonova adds no opacity policy and advances only its exact Eon pin to the immutable proof, so a config-free launch consumes `0.80`.

Important failures: invalid config behavior, changed Nova identity, an Eonova override, failed package/profile verification, or interruption of a live Session leaves the work incomplete.

## Evidence and decision

The user tested `0.8` through `~/.config/eon/config.toml` and explicitly selected it as the product default on 2026-08-14. Existing EON-C13 and Venus VEN-C11 already own the field, validation, launch argv, and default-background-only materialization. Published Eon proof `3149dfd92e6130f58ac7c086b6d90f9003c1c2df` and Eonova rollout `057d42b1b755c6ca25cd2f7012ac2de1ce069759` establish the exact correction and pin-only mechanisms.

Decision: change the one Eon `TerminalConfig::default` value and aligned expectations/current-state text, publish one new immutable Eon proof, then advance only Eonova Eon input/assertion and affected lock nodes. Preserve Venus, Orbit, Nova, configuration schema, wrapper, namespaces, and live generations. Add no dependency, setting layer, CLI flag, environment bridge, watcher, or Eonova override.

## Scope

In scope: EON-C13 default/current proof, existing default-consuming checks, README/CHANGELOG/LOC, exact Eon build/profile and installed proof; then trackerless Eonova exact Eon pin/lock, package/profile/boundary proof. This issue is the selected planning owner for both the correction and downstream Eonova rollout.

Out of scope: opacity semantics, explicit-cell transparency, blur, live mutation, child changes, Nova changes, config migration, another platform, or stopping existing supervisors.

## Acceptance Criteria\n
- Missing config and absent field yield `0.80`; explicit values and strict finite `0.0..=1.0` validation remain exact.
- Default Eon and EonTerm Venus argv carries `--background-opacity 0.8`.
- Locked Rust and exact Nix checks pass; Eon source, artifacts, contract proof, profile, and LOC are recorded.
- Eonova pins that exact Eon proof, retains Nova `9ef7f6530bac3b4296adbaa7b50eaef3c1716cf1`, remains override-free and Mars/Rio-free, and passes package, wrapper, desktop, license, closure, and profile checks.
- A config-free isolated Eonova launch observes Venus `--background-opacity 0.8`.
- Existing live Eonova supervisor, Orbit, and Venus PID/start identities remain unchanged.
- Only this issue metadata is published from the dirty Eon Beads file.

title: Accept native terminal text selection in Eon
description:
## Outcome and contract

Accept one exact Orbit and Venus pair that makes terminal text selection usable in installed Eon:

- Drag selects cells.
- Double-click and double-drag select words.
- Triple-click and triple-drag select logical lines.
- Terminal-owned mouse input remains unchanged; Shift forces host selection.
- Release copies to the Wayland primary selection.
- `Ctrl+Shift+C` copies to the ordinary clipboard.

Eon owns only exact component selection, launch integration, update policy, installed proof, and product defaults. Orbit Bead `orb-orbit-native-selection-gestures-qf3` owns terminal semantics. Venus Bead `ven-venus-native-selection-gestures-d3x` owns native input and clipboard effects.

This behavior refreshes the exact installed proofs for the existing EON-C1 through EON-C4 product contracts; it does not create an Eon-owned selection contract.

## Prerequisites and references

Required accepted children:

1. Eon Sessions `orb-orbit-native-selection-gestures-qf3`: exact ORBS and ORB-C9 selection proof.
2. Eon Desktop `ven-venus-native-selection-gestures-d3x`: exact VEN-C7 native input and Wayland clipboard proof.

Before implementation, compare the component manifest pins with both latest accepted child revisions and record the exact identities. Reuse the references and decisions recorded by the child owners. Inspect Eon's manifest, lock, Nix composition, launcher surfaces, profile update path, current EON-C1 through EON-C4 proof, and every packaged Eon, EonTerm, and Eonova entry point.

Impact: HIGH for daily terminal use. Effort: S after both children are accepted. Risk: LOW because Eon adds no selection mechanism. Confidence: HIGH.

## Implementation

1. Wait for both child Beads to close with immutable accepted revisions.
2. Update the canonical component graph and exact lock identities together; add no patch, adapter, fallback, feature flag, or duplicated schema.
3. Build and refresh the active Eon profile from the working tree without stopping live Sessions.
4. Verify each installed launcher consumes the just-built profile artifact.
5. Refresh EON-C1 through EON-C4 proof records, changelog, and LOC only for the accepted exact composition.

## Acceptance

- Manifest, lock, Cargo, and Nix identities resolve to the accepted Orbit and Venus revisions.
- Installed Eon and EonTerm demonstrate cell, word, and logical-line press-drag selection.
- A mouse-reporting application receives ordinary pointer input; Shift performs host selection.
- Release provides the exact frozen text through Wayland primary paste in another application.
- `Ctrl+Shift+C` updates the ordinary clipboard without conflating it with primary selection.
- Eonova launches against the same accepted Eon profile and demonstrates the same boundary.
- Closing and reopening launch surfaces preserves normal lifecycle behavior and does not disturb existing Sessions.
- The full affected Rust and Nix route, profile identity check, installed Wayland dogfood, governance checks, and `git diff --check` pass on one immutable candidate.
- Closure records exact Eon, Orbit, Venus, ORBS, package, profile, compositor, and platform identities plus user acceptance and remaining limits.

## Scope and stop conditions

In scope: exact child pins, canonical component graph and lock, Nix composition, installed launch surfaces, EON-C1 through EON-C4 proof refresh, changelog, LOC, and one accepted Wayland dogfood pass.

Out of scope: Eon-owned selection code, protocol translation, compatibility support, configuration, custom boundaries or timing, middle-click paste, right-click extension, block selection, drag autoscroll, OSC 133 command-output selection, other display systems, and other operating systems.

Stop if either child proof is incomplete or stale; if composition needs an Eon-side behavior patch, adapter, or second schema; if the profile cannot resolve exactly to the candidate; or if another active frontier owns the component graph.

title: Decide EonJS renderer-owned capture boundary
description:
## Contract Routing

- This is a planning and architecture decision. It changes no current `EON-C*`, `ORB-C*`, or `VEN-C*` contract and creates no runtime behavior, repository, module, dependency, protocol, language, or compatibility promise.
- `EonJS` is a working label for a possible future **Eon for the web** renderer. The accepted public/repository naming remains `Eon for the web` / `eon-web`; closure must decide the durable technical name and owner before implementation.
- Orbit remains the sole process, PTY, terminal-emulation, terminal-state, attachment, terminal-query, and semantic-input-encoding owner.
- Eon remains the workspace, lifecycle, composition, compatibility, and product-policy owner. Venus remains the native rendering owner. A future web client may own its own pixels but must not become another terminal authority.
- Implementation requires a separately activated owner-specific Bead after exact contract, language/toolchain, reference, dependency, portability, and active-frontier approval.

## Why

A future Eon web renderer could make deterministic screenshots and recordings a nearly free output target of the actual product renderer. If capture is added later as a separate renderer, it would duplicate font/layout/compositing policy and could disagree with the displayed Eon surface. If it is treated as a terminal emulator, it would also violate Orbit authority. The decision is cheap before a web renderer exists and expensive after its rendering boundary hardens.

Effort: S for the decision. Implementation effort is intentionally unestimated until the renderer and protocol boundary exist. Risk: MED because this crosses a future repository, language/toolchain, rendering, and Orbit-client boundary. Confidence: HIGH in the ownership constraint; MED in the future implementation shape.

## Evidence

- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:11-20,65-93` assigns PTY and terminal state to Orbit, native rendering to Venus, workspace policy to Eon, and forbids Eon from implementing terminal parsing or rendering.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:38-41` reserves `Eon for the web` / `eon-web` for a separately implemented future client.
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md:18` proves `EON-C4`: Eon adds no duplicate terminal or rendering state.
- `AGENTS.md:252-259` requires explicit user approval before durable TypeScript or another implementation language is added.
- `AGENTS.md:286-302` permits research and Beads to prepare a later frontier but forbids implementation against speculative child APIs.
- Joshka Betamax at exact main revision `7fbaa1598e3601ccb60f244a8c669d60a6d780db` demonstrates an efficient PTY → `libghostty-vt` → persistent renderer → in-process PNG/GIF/state pipeline without tmux, a browser, or termshot. It is a comparison, not a dependency or source-reuse choice.
- Ghostty discussion `#12610`, answered 2026-05-12, records the material limitation: `libghostty-vt` exposes render state but no single canonical Ghostty pixel output; consumers own rendering.
- Related decision `eon-pxn.7` asks whether Eon owns agent-driven terminal-testing behavior. It may later consume a capture surface, but neither decision blocks or implies the other.

## Decision Question

If the user activates Eon for the web, should its actual product renderer be the sole terminal-to-pixel owner for both interactive presentation and deterministic capture, exposing an offscreen RGBA/PNG target from the same render path, or should Eon rely on external capture tooling?

## Smallest Candidate Contract

- Consumer: a future Eon for the web client and an explicitly authorized local capture caller.
- Trigger: the renderer has accepted one exact source-labeled Orbit presentation revision plus fixed render configuration, and the caller requests a bounded capture.
- Result: the same renderer path used for interactive presentation renders an offscreen surface and returns bounded RGBA or PNG with renderer, frame, font, theme, scale, dimensions, and clock identity sufficient to reproduce or reject the artifact.
- Important failures: incompatible or stale presentation revision, incomplete state, missing or mismatched font/resource, unsupported graphic, invalid dimensions, surface/readback failure, cancellation, timeout, and encoder failure are explicit and produce no falsely authoritative artifact.
- Authority: the artifact proves the selected web renderer's pixels only. It does not prove native Venus pixels or a universal Ghostty/Eon appearance.

## Scope

In scope:
- Decide whether built-in renderer-owned capture is part of a future Eon for the web boundary.
- Compare no built-in capture, external Betamax-like tooling, actual-renderer offscreen capture, native Venus offscreen capture, and compositor/window capture.
- Decide the owner and minimum boundary for presentation-state consumption, deterministic rendering inputs, offscreen pixels, artifact metadata, encoding, cancellation, cleanup, and failure reporting.
- Decide whether TypeScript/JavaScript and a browser, Node, Deno, WASM, Canvas, WebGPU, or another runtime removes enough complete responsibility to justify its toolchain and portability cost.
- Select at most one disposable proof, or record that external tooling is sufficient.

Out of scope:
- Implementing EonJS, `eon-web`, a renderer, capture API, tape language, recorder CLI, GIF/video encoder, browser server, agent harness, MCP/plugin surface, CI job, or remote service.
- Creating another PTY owner, VT parser, terminal emulator, Orbit schema mirror, raw-PTY consumer, OCR authority, or concurrent input-capable Orbit client.
- Claiming pixel identity with Venus, Ghostty, arbitrary terminals, operating-system compositors, or different font/platform stacks.
- Choosing arbitrary split trees, broader web access, authentication, collaboration, persistence, streaming, or distribution.

## Reference And Tool Gates

At activation, inspect exact accepted Orbit and Eon protocol revisions, the selected web-renderer candidates, Joshka Betamax `7fbaa1598e3601ccb60f244a8c669d60a6d780db`, and Ghostty discussion `#12610`. Resolve any named `RioTermJS` reference to an exact repository and revision before using it; an unresolved project name is not evidence. Record adopted mechanisms, rejected surrounding scope, licenses, owned LOC, transitive/build/native cost, platform support, headless behavior, font determinism, accessibility implications, upgrade burden, and replacement cost.

## Sequencing

- Status remains deferred until the user activates the Eon for the web product decision.
- This has no hard dependency on `eon-pxn.7`; that agent-testing decision may later consume an accepted capture contract.
- Stop before adding or changing any contract, repository, module, implementation language, dependency, or active frontier without explicit user approval.

## Verification

- `br show <id> --json` should show one deferred, unclaimed decision with the complete boundary and no blocking dependency.
- `br sync --flush-only` should exit 0.
- `git diff --check` should exit 0; only Beads planning state may change.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Closure explicitly decides whether Eon for the web and its renderer are accepted product scope, records the durable technical/repository owner, and does not treat the working label `EonJS` as prior approval.
2. The record chooses renderer-owned offscreen capture or explicit external-tool sufficiency after comparing: no built-in capture, Joshka Betamax-like external capture, future web-renderer capture, native Venus offscreen capture, and compositor/window capture.
3. If renderer-owned capture is selected, one observable contract names the consumer, accepted presentation revision and render configuration trigger, RGBA/PNG result, artifact identity, bounds, cancellation, cleanup, and explicit failures.
4. Interactive and offscreen output use one renderer owner and one terminal-to-pixel path. No screenshot-specific renderer reconstructs font, layout, cursor, graphics, palette, or compositing policy.
5. Orbit remains the sole process, PTY, terminal-emulation, terminal-state, attachment, query, and semantic-input-encoding owner. The selected shape consumes one exact accepted Orbit presentation contract and maintains no raw-PTY path, VT parser, second emulator, or handwritten schema mirror.
6. Eon remains the workspace, lifecycle, composition, authorization, and compatibility owner. Venus retains native rendering. Capture artifacts are explicitly authoritative only for the selected web renderer, not Venus, Ghostty, arbitrary terminals, or every platform/font stack.
7. Deterministic capture inputs cover renderer revision, source frame revision, font/resource identity, theme, dimensions, scale, and controlled presentation time. Unsupported or missing inputs fail rather than silently substituting a falsely reproducible artifact.
8. Encoding stays downstream of terminal rendering. PNG is the first proof surface; an existing bounded encoder such as ffmpeg is preferred for GIF/video unless measurement proves an in-process encoder removes enough lifecycle cost to own.
9. The language/tool gate compares Rust/no new language with any proposed TypeScript/JavaScript, browser, Node, Deno, WASM, Canvas, or WebGPU shape. Closure records platform/headless support, owned LOC, direct/transitive/build/native cost, license, security posture, upgrade burden, replacement cost, and explicit user approval before any durable second language or toolchain.
10. Reference closure records exact inspected Orbit/Eon contracts, Joshka Betamax `7fbaa1598e3601ccb60f244a8c669d60a6d780db`, Ghostty discussion `#12610`, and exact revisions for every adopted renderer candidate. An unresolved `RioTermJS` name is not accepted evidence.
11. The decision selects at most one disposable end-to-end proof and names its cheapest falsifying check, expected failure behavior, portability disposition, and evidence that would reverse the choice. It creates no production code, contract, module, repository, dependency, tape DSL, encoder, browser service, agent harness, plugin/MCP surface, CI job, remote service, or compatibility promise.
12. Any accepted implementation is deferred to separately user-activated owner-specific Beads after exact contracts and one-active-frontier sequencing exist. `eon-pxn.7` remains related but non-blocking; neither issue silently expands the other.
notes:
Ghostty WebAssembly and snapshot comparison — 2026-08-15:
- Exact primary source: Ghostty revision d760ee96e54657416eb427b793c7e839f003df7d, including README.md, example/wasm-vt, include/ghostty/vt/snapshot.h, src/terminal/snapshot, and .github/workflows/release-tip.yml. Mitchell Hashimoto's benchmark post is https://x.com/mitchellh/status/2088378990998524206.
- Evidence: libghostty-vt builds for wasm32-freestanding and exposes terminal, render-state, key, selection, snapshot, and allocator functions through a low-level C ABI. The snapshot is an ordered CRC32C-protected record stream with a renderable READY prefix, unfinished VT/UTF-8 continuation, later history pages, and FINISH. Snapshot v1 has no binary-compatibility guarantee and omits Kitty image and placement state. The module supplies no renderer, PTY, transport, authentication, font, accessibility, or browser product shell.
- Performance disposition: the published Apple M4 Max comparison measures VT writes, resize/reflow, and render-state preparation against current xterm.js. Full and incremental render comparisons reuse xterm.js's WebGL model and exclude drawing and GPU work. Treat the result as candidate-selection evidence, not Eon browser latency, memory, accessibility, or compatibility proof.
- Decision effect: keep a thin exact-version ORBF consumer as the default candidate. Compare checkpoint-plus-ordered-tail replication only if a measured transport, bootstrap, or render-state cost makes structured frames insufficient. A browser replica must remain non-authoritative; Orbit alone answers terminal queries and owns process, PTY, parser, modes, history, selection, and effects. Any relaxation requires a separate Orbit replication contract rather than this capture decision.
- Artifact gate: upstream publishes signed optimized files through a moving nightly release and states that libghostty API signatures remain in flux. Do not select a nightly URL, snapshot v1, WebAssembly SIMD requirement, JavaScript wrapper, or artifact-distribution policy as an Eon contract.
- Rejected scope: xterm.js replacement work, Eon for the web activation, a second terminal emulator or schema owner, raw PTY delivery, browser transport/authentication, and performance claims derived from the upstream chart.
- Cheapest later comparison: feed one bounded recorded corpus through the accepted native Orbit owner and a disposable exact-revision WASM candidate; compare canonical cells, modes, continuation, reflow, alternate screen, effects and declared unsupported graphics, then measure total bootstrap/update cost. Delete the proof if thin ORBF remains sufficient.

title: Expose caller-owned application identity through EonTerm
description:
## Outcome and contract

Fix the observed native-Wayland launcher collision by giving each Eon surface the application identity owned by its caller before Venus creates the window. This implementation creates `VEN-C17` and `EON-C16`; the user's 2026-08-24 instruction “fix it” approves this exact Eonova-driven contract.

- Consumer: full Eon, standalone EonTerm, or one approved EonTerm composition.
- Trigger: launch a new native terminal surface through Eon/EonTerm; an approved composition may supply one validated desktop application ID.
- Result: full Eon uses `eon`, standalone EonTerm uses `eonterm`, and Eonova supplies `eonova`. Eon passes the selected value unchanged to Venus before window creation; Venus maps it through exact winit `WindowAttributesExtWayland::with_name`, whose general name is the Wayland app ID. Each value matches the corresponding desktop-file basename where one exists, so launchers can distinguish Eonova from an already-running Eon window.
- Failures: an absent consumer override uses the mode-owned default; a non-UTF-8, empty, oversized, or non-token identity fails before Orbit or Venus starts. A profile refresh never mutates an already-running surface; that supervisor keeps its original identity until the user closes or stops it.

Eon owns defaults, validation, the EonTerm invocation surface, and the one-way launch value. Venus owns only native mapping and retains `eon` as its direct-invocation default. Eonova owns only its fixed `eonova` choice and matching desktop metadata. Orbit titles, PTY state, child argv/environment, and Session lifetime remain unchanged.

## Minimum shape

1. Add one optional `--application-id ID` argument to Venus and project it through the existing launch structure into `with_name`; keep the direct default `eon`.
2. Add one optional `--application-id ID` before EonTerm's `-- COMMAND...`; full Eon supplies `eon`, bare EonTerm supplies `eonterm`, and Eon passes exactly one value to Venus for initial and replacement presentation processes.
3. Update Eonova's existing wrapper to pass `--application-id eonova` and change its desktop `StartupWMClass` to `eonova` so metadata is honest on systems that consult it.
4. Update contract/help/current-state docs and exact pins in owner order: Venus, Eon, Eonova.

Reuse the existing parser, launch struct, `venus_command`, winit native seam, wrapper, and desktop item. Add no dependency, protocol version, registry, branding object, mutable identity, title coupling, environment inference, command inspection, desktop-file loading, or second launcher path.

## References and evidence

Required and inspected before code:

- Exact winit source at patched 0.30.13 commit `fb45fbf901fbe70cc9a877b5d651d0b60c206b08`: Wayland `with_name(general, instance)` maps `general` to xdg-toplevel app ID and ignores `instance`.
- Freedesktop Desktop Entry specification: application names/desktop IDs use an ASCII desktop-file-compatible identity and window app IDs should match the desktop-file basename.
- Venus `cd2c63363d670e27f09c26d3c8889d2849eabaec`: `application.rs` hardcodes `with_name("eon", "yazelix-venus")`; `launch.rs` already owns bounded CLI parsing before window creation.
- Eon `4a89960c17877e072cd23fa5ceab1e2cfd285da9`: `cli.rs` owns EonTerm invocation and `supervisor.rs::venus_command` owns every initial/replacement Venus argv. Current accepted Venus source pin is `ee3defea55c77f7acc4559606965d93d39bba8b5`.
- Eonova `d8a8729f442f3d535b30fd22ac8dc7b6da4626dd`: wrapper selects a private runtime namespace but passes no application identity; both Eon and Eonova desktop entries advertise `StartupWMClass=yazelix-venus`. Reproduced on COSMIC Wayland: the desktop entry's exact executable is valid and direct launch starts EonTerm, Orbit, Venus, and Nova, while shared native identity prevents reliable launcher distinction.

Rejected: changing only `StartupWMClass` while Venus still publishes app ID `eon`; deriving identity from child argv, executable name, environment, title, icon, or runtime path; adding product knowledge to Venus; changing Orbit/EONW protocols; a general branding framework; supporting X11/Xwayland or other platforms.

Portability disposition: neutral bounded identity value with one isolated native Wayland mapping. This creates no additional platform promise.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Venus deterministically accepts its direct `eon` default and one valid caller ID, rejects invalid values before window creation, and applies the accepted ID to the native Wayland attributes while title updates remain independent.
2. Full Eon launches Venus with `eon`; bare EonTerm launches it with `eonterm`; `eonterm --application-id eonova -- COMMAND...` launches initial and replacement Venus processes with `eonova` without exposing the value to the PTY child.
3. Existing decoration, opacity, blur, cursor, socket, presentation, repeat-launch, recovery, and Session-lifecycle behavior remains exact. No wire contract changes.
4. Eonova's wrapper supplies `eonova`, its desktop metadata matches, and package/runtime namespaces remain unchanged and isolated.
5. Focused parser/argv checks, full affected locked Rust checks, Eon and Eonova Nix checks/builds, desktop validation, closure/license checks, LOC scorecards, and `git diff --check` pass.
6. After exact owner commits/pins and profile refreshes, native Wayland dogfood shows Open Eon and Eonova as distinct launcher/running-window identities. Repeated Eonova launch presents the existing Eonova surface rather than focusing Eon or creating a second Session.

## Scope boundary and stop conditions

In scope: one bounded ID string, Eon/EonTerm defaults, the existing Venus Wayland window-attribute seam, Eonova's fixed wrapper/desktop metadata, exact pins, docs, tests, and installed proof.

Out of scope: mutable identity, per-generation identity negotiation, branding/icons, a provider registry, desktop-entry discovery, X11/Xwayland/macOS, new distribution channels, or changes to Orbit, EONW, Nova, Zellij, or live Session ownership.

Stop and return to the user if the existing one-way launch value cannot fix COSMIC without a runtime/wire protocol, a second identity/branding structure, a new dependency, or changes outside Venus, Eon, and Eonova composition metadata.
close_reason: Installed distinct Eonova identity and crash-residue recovery accepted by user on native COSMIC Wayland.

title: Expose terminal background opacity
description:
## Approved outcome and contract

The user approved this opacity-first Eon shape on 2026-08-14 America/Sao_Paulo. This implementation creates `EON-C13` after indexing the approved contract before code and consumes exact accepted Venus `VEN-C11`.

- Consumer: a local Eon or EonTerm user and an approved composition such as Eonova.
- Trigger: create or reopen a Venus surface while the canonical Eon configuration root contains `[terminal] background_opacity = VALUE`, or contains no such value.
- Result: Eon accepts one finite `f32` in `0.0..=1.0`, defaults absence to `0.90`, and passes the exact typed value through the existing Venus launch boundary as `--background-opacity VALUE`. Full Eon and EonTerm use the same setting. An already open Venus remains unchanged; after that presentation process exits, `eon attach` or `eonterm attach` starts a new Venus with the current value while preserving the live Orbit Session and PTY child.
- Failures: an invalid field identifies `terminal.background_opacity` and fails before initial Orbit or Venus process creation. A bad value read while reopening Venus returns a bounded presentation failure and never stops the existing Orbit Session or child.

This creates `EON-C13`, consumes exact `VEN-C11`, hardens `EON-C1` through `EON-C4` and `EON-C12`, and preserves `EON-C8` through `EON-C11`. Eon owns schema, bounds, default, configuration diagnostics, apply timing, generation/lifecycle policy, and exact child compatibility. Venus owns native validation and materialization. Orbit remains unaware of opacity.

Impact: HIGH. Effort: M. Implementation risk: LOW/MED. Confidence: HIGH in the existing parser and reopen boundaries.

## Evidence

- `crates/eon/src/managed_environment.rs:10-31`: the existing strict serde/TOML `EonConfig` owner currently contains only `[shell]` and denies unknown fields.
- `crates/eon/src/managed_environment.rs:222-244`: configuration is read from the canonical Eon root and already produces bounded field-specific diagnostics.
- `crates/eon/src/main.rs:1127-1180`: a new generation prepares configuration before starting the supervisor and children.
- `crates/eon/src/main.rs:1374-1384`: `venus_command` is the single Eon-to-Venus argv owner and currently forwards decorations and socket endpoints.
- `crates/eon/src/main.rs:1893-1920`: Present preserves a live Venus or starts a new presentation for the existing first Session when Venus has exited.
- `crates/eon/src/main.rs:1530-1645`: the supervisor keeps Orbit Sessions alive after Venus exits.
- Existing Venus issue `ven-terminal-presentation-settings-5y7` owns the approved `VEN-C11` background semantics and exact native alpha behavior.
- Eonova `247265c44f759f8142783af7dfd5415c25211c5c` adds no opacity override around EonTerm, so it inherits the Eon default once its exact Eon pin includes EON-C13.

## Minimum product shape

1. Extend the existing strict `EonConfig` with one `TerminalConfig { background_opacity: f32 }`; use `0.90` as the serde/default value. Add no profile framework, new parser, config crate, dependency, or settings service.
2. Validate finiteness and `0.0..=1.0` in the Eon config owner. Preserve exact unknown-field rejection and identify the canonical field in all errors.
3. Validate the configuration before initial child creation. Re-read only the terminal setting at the existing `start_venus` boundary so a presentation reopened by the supervisor sees the current file. Do not reread or restart Orbit.
4. Pass the exact value to the accepted Venus CLI boundary on every Eon-owned Venus creation. Keep direct child argv construction in `venus_command`; add no environment-variable-per-setting boundary or serialized generic profile.
5. Keep the public `eonterm` command shape unchanged. Configuration is the public owner; a one-off opacity CLI flag is not part of this slice.
6. Document one authoritative field, its range, 0.90 default, apply-on-reopen timing, and terminal-background-only semantics in current Eon help/docs. Do not build a generic configuration-inventory protocol for one field. Exact-version consumers pin and consume `EON-C13`.
7. After an immutable source candidate, update contract proof metadata, README LOC, and CHANGELOG for the accepted configuration and behavior, then close through the repository source-proof workflow.

## Ownership and behavior limits

- Eon base default is `0.90`; Eonova deliberately provides no override and consumes this value.
- The setting controls terminal default background opacity through Venus. It does not make text, cursor, explicit terminal cell backgrounds, workspace chrome, native decorations, or the input region transparent.
- Visual transparency does not imply click-through.
- Live watching and mutation of an already open Venus are excluded because X11 requires the transparent window shape at creation and one cross-platform reopen rule is sufficient.
- Nova root appearance and Zellij themes remain Nova-owned. Orbit terminal colors and cursor state remain Orbit-owned.

## Prerequisites and references

Local prerequisite `eon-4is.4` is closed. External prerequisite: Venus `ven-terminal-presentation-settings-5y7` proves the approved `VEN-C11` at an exact revision before Eon changes its launch boundary.

Required before code: current `AGENTS.md`; complete issue and comments; `docs/CONTRACTS.md`; current config, launch, supervisor, presentation, attach, manifest, help, and diagnostics owners; exact accepted `VEN-C11`; existing Eon child revision freshness policy; and Eonova source only to verify the absence of an opacity override.

No dependency is selected. A parser, manifest, or other dependency change requires the repository crate gate and user approval.

Platform disposition: neutral configuration and lifecycle policy over the isolated Venus platform owner. Linux is proved first. Eon does not claim macOS transparency until Venus proves the exact native capability.

## Acceptance

1. The approved `EON-C13` row is indexed before code and names exact accepted `VEN-C11` plus the child update order.
2. No config file and an absent field both yield `0.90`. Exact `0.0`, `0.90`, and `1.0` are accepted. NaN, infinity, negative, greater-than-one, wrong-type, duplicate, and unknown terminal fields fail with `terminal.background_opacity` in the diagnostic.
3. Initial invalid configuration fails before Orbit, Venus, sockets, or a supervisor generation is created.
4. Every Eon-owned Venus launch receives one exact `--background-opacity VALUE` before the socket endpoints. Workspace and EonTerm launch agree and existing decoration behavior remains exact.
5. A changed configuration does not mutate or replace a live Venus. After Venus exits, `eon attach` or `eonterm attach` reads the current value and opens a replacement Venus against the same live Orbit Session and PTY child. Invalid reopen configuration leaves those processes alive and reports presentation unavailable.
6. Eon documents the exact field, range, default, owner, terminal-background-only layer policy, and reopen timing without importing Mars configuration or promising live reload.
7. Focused tests cover strict parsing, defaulting, finite/range validation, exact argv for workspace/EonTerm and decorations, initial failure ordering, reopen re-read, presentation failure, and preserved Orbit/child identity.
8. Installed Linux dogfood covers default `0.90`, explicit `0.88`, full transparency `0.0`, Eon and EonTerm, decorated and undecorated Venus, close-and-attach reopen, invalid edit, long-running child survival, resize, reconnect, selection, IME, and accessibility.
9. Closure records exact Eon and Venus revisions, contract ids, config/argv examples, process identities across reopen, checks, dependency disposition, portability, LOC, and remaining compositor/macOS limits.

## Verification

- Focused config and launch/lifecycle tests must fail before implementation and prove all accepted boundaries.
- `cargo fmt --check`
- `cargo check --locked`
- `cargo test --locked`
- `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo run --locked -p eon-manifest -- --check`
- `git diff --check`

Run repository Nix/package checks required by the final changed surface and record exact success. All proof commands must target one materially unchanged candidate.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if Venus `VEN-C11` is not accepted at an exact revision or Eon would need a compatibility window.
- Stop before a new dependency, generic profile or inventory framework, environment-variable-per-setting boundary, public one-off CLI option, live watcher, Orbit restart, PTY replacement, or another product-default change.
- Stop for user choice before explicit-cell opacity, blur, workspace glass, click-through, macOS behavior, or another presentation field enters this contract.
- Stop if another active implementation owns the same config, launch, supervisor, or child revision surfaces.

## Maintenance notes

The deferred typography and initial-geometry outcome is tracked separately. Do not expand this issue merely because the `[terminal]` section exists.

title: Evaluate Rust quality tools across Eon projects
description:
## Contract routing

This repository-tooling research changes no EON, ORB, or VEN product contract, runtime behavior, dependency, package, compatibility promise, or proof status.

Consumer: the Eon maintainer choosing proportionate Rust verification for Eon, Eon Sessions and Eon Desktop.

Trigger: deciding whether the Rust tools already owned by the local Home Manager configuration should become recurring project evidence.

Result: bounded measurements at exact repository revisions produce one durable disposition for each tool, including scope, cadence, owner, cost, limitations and the condition that would justify repository packaging.

Important failures: do not mistake a runner or metric for an independent correctness oracle; do not impose whole-workspace mutation, coverage, fuzzing, Miri, CI, Nix or developer-environment policy without evidence; do not alter product source or contracts; do not include Rust tooling in Nix-only Eonova.

## Required evidence

Before measurement, read the complete current AGENTS.md for all three Rust repositories, inspect their Cargo workspaces, tests, unsafe and FFI surfaces, existing verification commands and exact Home Manager tool ownership. Use installed tool help and exact local versions as primary operational evidence. Consult upstream primary documentation only if local behavior is ambiguous.

Adopt existing fmt, check, test and strict Clippy as the baseline owner. Treat cargo-llvm-cov plus cargo-crap, cargo-mutants, cargo-udeps and cargo-fuzz as candidates for narrower evidence. Treat nextest, watch, sweep, tokei and Miri as comparison or rejected project scope unless measurement overturns the reason.

## Method

1. Record exact HEAD, dirty state, Rust/tool versions and relevant workspace shape for Eon, Eon Sessions and Eon Desktop.
2. Run bounded coverage/CRAP evidence, mutation discovery plus one representative deterministic mutation slice per applicable repository, and unused-dependency analysis. Record command, result, wall time, useful signal, noise and unexercised surfaces.
3. In Eon Sessions, inspect and at most build/list the existing codec fuzz surface; do not conduct an unbounded fuzz campaign.
4. Evaluate nextest, watch, sweep, tokei and Miri by the responsibility they own and the repository surfaces they can actually prove.
5. Record one final matrix: adopt, optional personal tool, targeted existing Bead, or reject for now. Name cadence, scope and promotion/reversal conditions.
6. Leave project source, manifests, Nix, docs, contracts and child-repository Beads unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria

- Exact revisions, environment, commands, results and observed wall time are recorded for every executed measurement.
- Coverage/CRAP, mutants, udeps and fuzz receive evidence-backed scoped dispositions; negative results and tool failures are retained.
- The decision explicitly preserves the universal fmt/check/test/Clippy baseline, keeps machine housekeeping and feedback-loop tools personal, and excludes Eonova.
- Repository packaging is rejected until repeated value demonstrates a reproducibility problem worth owning.
- No implementation or tracked project file changes; only this Eon Bead may change.
- br lint, git diff --check and br sync --flush-only pass before closure.

## Stop conditions

Stop or narrow a measurement if a repository source surface changes concurrently, a command would interrupt live Eon Sessions, a tool requires a new dependency or checked-in configuration, or a bounded run cannot finish without becoming a benchmark project. Record the limit rather than widening scope.
notes:
Completed decision — 2026-08-14

The user selected this single cross-repository research outcome after accepting the proposed tool split. Exact evidence and commands are retained in comment 488.

Final disposition:

- Universal project gate: retain only the existing locked cargo fmt, check, test and strict Clippy commands. They remain the canonical routine verification owner.
- cargo-llvm-cov plus cargo-crap: adopt as periodic advisory evidence after substantial parser, protocol, reducer, state-machine or test changes and during bounded audit or release preparation. Always pair CRAP with real LCOV. Inspect deltas and concrete functions; impose no absolute coverage or CRAP threshold. Reconsider a gate only after repeated exact-revision runs show stable source matching, low noise and a threshold correlated with confirmed defects.
- cargo-mutants: adopt only as a file or function bounded test-strength check for deterministic contracts and known regressions. Record the selected mutation set and timeout. Never run the 703, 1101 or 1694 whole-workspace sets as a routine gate without new measured need.
- cargo-udeps: adopt as a periodic manual dependency check after manifest or feature changes and before a release or dependency audit. Use nightly, all targets and locked resolution; manually review target and feature false positives. Do not add it per edit or to hosted automation on this evidence.
- cargo-fuzz: route only through existing Sessions Bead orb-fuzz-orbit-codecs-kf5 for canonical ORBS and ORBF decoder campaigns. Do not create Eon, Venus, full-server or continuous fuzz scope. The existing Bead owns whether a minimum tracked harness is eventually justified.
- cargo-nextest: optional local runner for Eon and Desktop only. It is not an independent quality oracle and must not replace cargo test. Reject it as a default Sessions runner because its default concurrency failed an Orbit lifecycle test while the canonical exact cargo test passed.
- Miri: reject for now. The component is unavailable locally and the important unsafe boundaries are native PTY, libc and libghostty FFI seams better exercised by existing process and integration checks. Reconsider only when a pure-Rust unsafe owner appears with a Miri-compatible contract.
- cargo-watch, cargo-sweep-all and tokei: keep personal. Watch owns feedback-loop convenience, sweep owns machine storage housekeeping, and tokei owns counting; none proves project correctness.
- Eonova: include no Rust quality tools because it has no Rust workspace.

Tool ownership and promotion condition:

Home Manager remains the single owner of installed developer tools. Add no repository Nix, devShell, manifest, configuration, CI or documentation surface. A separately user-selected tooling Bead becomes justified only after repeated accepted use demonstrates either a second-machine reproducibility failure or a recurring contributor command whose value exceeds its packaging and maintenance cost.

No product contract, proof status, runtime behavior, dependency, package or compatibility promise changed. No implementation or child-repository planning item was created or updated.

title: Preserve native Fish completions when enabling Carapace
description:
## Contract routing

Harden accepted EON-C9 for managed Fish. A Fish user is the consumer; native `config.fish` registers per-command completions and Eon's Carapace toggle is enabled; Eon must preserve those native registrations while adding the pinned Carapace fallback for commands without user-owned coverage. A disabled toggle must remain inert. This changes no configuration field, default, shell command, or Carapace-owned semantics.

## Why

Eon sources Carapace's generated Fish init after native configuration. The exact generator clears every existing completion for each command it claims before installing `_carapace_completer`, so native per-command completions silently disappear despite the accepted preservation rule.

Impact: MEDIUM. Effort: S/M. Implementation risk: MEDIUM. Confidence: HIGH.

## Evidence

- `flake.nix:263-279`: Eon generates the exact Carapace Fish init.
- `flake.nix:476-478`: the managed Fish adapter sources that init after native `config.fish` without preserving existing registrations.
- Carapace 1.6.3 `cmd/carapace/cmd/lazyinit/fish.go:28-33` emits `complete -e` for each claimed command before registering `_carapace_completer`.
- `eon-audit-eon-managed-environment-hay`: an isolated native `complete -c git -a eon_user_marker` disappears when only Eon's Carapace integration is enabled.
- The accepted EON-C9 proof claims an existing native completer and per-command Fish completions survive managed fallback activation.

## Prerequisite and reference gate

- Blocked by `eon-generated-runtime-identity-h4g`; the generated-adapter correction must select a fresh supervisor after a profile update.
- Before code, record the execution baseline and read the complete closed audit, EON-C9 proof, exact Fish 4.7.1 completion/startup documentation and implementation, exact Carapace 1.6.3 Fish lazy-init source, and current generated adapter.
- Nova remains comparison-only. Do not import its shell framework or broaden this fix beyond Fish completion preservation.
- Record adopted native Fish mechanisms and rejected surrounding Carapace/Nova scope in the Bead reference gate.
- No dependency or crate feature is expected. Stop for the crate gate and user approval before any manifest change.

## Scope

In scope:
- The Fish-specific generated adapter in `flake.nix` and the minimum isolated regression for native completion preservation plus Carapace fallback activation.
- Current-state EON-C9 proof metadata, CHANGELOG, and README LOC where required by the accepted fix.

Out of scope:
- Nushell, Bash, Zsh, prompt, history, directory jumping, shell ownership, or new integration toggles.
- Reimplementing Carapace completion logic, parsing its command database, patching upstream Carapace, or adding a shell framework.
- Changing user `config.fish`, command startup order beyond the minimum preservation boundary, or behavior when Carapace is disabled.
- Adding dependencies or compatibility promises.

Platform classification: neutral shell-startup policy with isolated current Nix generation; no new macOS blocker.

## Implementation notes

1. Write one isolated failing Fish regression before changing the adapter: native config registers a unique marker for `git`, only Carapace is enabled, and post-startup inspection must still contain the marker.
2. Around the existing generated Carapace init, use Fish's native completion introspection/definitions to preserve pre-existing registrations for claimed commands. Keep the generated Carapace init itself authoritative for fallback behavior.
3. Avoid a custom completion parser or a maintained command list. Reuse the exact generated init and restore only user/native state it displaced.
4. Also prove a command without pre-existing completion retains Carapace's `_carapace_completer` registration and the disabled toggle performs no Carapace initialization.
5. Advance EON-C9 proof metadata after the proof-bearing commit and refresh the installed runtime without stopping older generations.

## Acceptance

- An isolated native `complete -c git -a eon_user_marker` remains visible after managed Fish starts with only Carapace enabled.
- A command with no pre-existing native completion retains the pinned Carapace fallback registration.
- Repeated interactive startup does not duplicate or progressively alter preserved completion definitions.
- Native Fish configuration still runs before Eon's guarded integrations; Carapace disabled remains inert.
- Starship, Zoxide, Atuin, PATH, argv, environment filtering, and other shells retain their observable behavior.
- No new dependency, command list, shell framework, public configuration, or contract is introduced.

## Verification

- One isolated Fish completion regression should fail before the fix and exit 0 after proving both native marker preservation and Carapace fallback coverage.
- Existing managed Fish adapter tests should exit 0 with unchanged non-completion signals.
- `cargo fmt --check`
- `cargo check --locked`
- `cargo test --locked`
- `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo run --locked -p eon-manifest -- components/eon-alpha-v1.json`
- `nix build --no-link --print-out-paths --no-update-lock-file path:.#default`
- `nix flake check --no-update-lock-file path:.`
- `git diff --check`
- Installed profile and `eon versions` checks after the accepted proof commit.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if the cited Fish/Carapace mechanism or EON-C9 ownership has drifted materially.
- Stop if preservation requires parsing unstable human output, maintaining a Carapace command list, patching upstream, or changing native user configuration.
- Stop if the candidate merely moves Carapace earlier and thereby changes which completion source wins without preserving both accepted behaviors.
- Stop before adding a dependency, new configuration surface, broader shell policy, or cross-repository change.
- Stop if the same verification failure repeats twice after a reasonable correction.

## Maintenance notes

This is a Fish adapter boundary fix, not an integration framework. Preserve native definitions around the exact upstream-generated init; do not fork Carapace or duplicate its command ownership.
close_reason: Exact Fish correction preserves native completions, retains Carapace fallback, passes committed proof, and leaves seven live Sessions intact.

title: Stop spawned Sessions whose Ready identity is rejected
description:
## Contract routing

Hardens EON-C1 launch failure and EON-C15 pre-lease rollback by consuming accepted ORB-C13 owner proof `2518512758c7848bbd87f907b105c8bcf0fc4e1b`. Before Ready, only a launcher-held exact empty record claim authorizes local Child rollback. After Orbit marks that retained inode, Eon uses only canonical management Stop on a matching spawned-child Live identity and never Child/PID fallback. Changes no Orbit, Venus, EONW, or workspace topology contract.

## Why

The original `eon-g3k` work fixed rejected Live identity cleanup but inferred the Ready boundary from record observations. Orbit can publish between the final absent-record observation and local Child stop. Accepted `orb-h1f` supplies the exact-inode lock-and-marker owner boundary needed to remove that race.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start Orbit while Eon retains local-child rollback authority.
2. Let Orbit mark or publish Ready after Eon observes no canonical record but before Eon acts on a startup failure.
3. Observe that an inferred `published` flag can authorize Child SIGKILL after Orbit owns the run, bypassing management cleanup.

## Scope

In scope:
- exact Orbit pin `2518512758c7848bbd87f907b105c8bcf0fc4e1b` in the canonical component graph and derived Cargo/Nix locks
- `crates/eon/src/main.rs` retained Ready claim and `start_orbit` rollback
- `crates/eon/tests/workspace_control.rs` managed helper and regression coverage
- CHANGELOG, EON-C1/EON-C15 proof state, README LOC, Nix profiles

Out of scope:
- Child/PID/signal fallback after Ready
- recovering or killing foreign Live records
- Orbit or Venus source changes, Venus pin changes, EONW, workspace topology
- module-splitting Beads or implementation

## Acceptance Criteria

- Eon creates and retains the exact empty owned 0600 record claim before spawning Orbit.
- A launcher-held empty claim is the sole pre-Ready Child rollback authority and is held through local stop.
- A marked claim permanently forbids Child/PID fallback even if Live later disappears; a matching spawned-child Live record may be stopped only through management.
- Rejected Ready identity leaves no live helper or record, and retry reaches the existing Venus-launch failure path.
- Exact Orbit pin/locks, full Rust/Nix surfaces, refreshed `eon` and `eonterm` profiles, and the cheapest installed behavior check pass without interrupting live Sessions.

## Reference Gate

Consume the accepted ORB-C13 exact-inode claim contract and proof. Preserve EON-C15 one-owner rollback, Orbit ORB-C12 shutdown, FrankenTerm lifecycle-boundary evidence, and Process Triage observe/act serialization. Reject a directory lock, inferred boolean Ready state, Child kill after a marker, record deletion without an Orbit tombstone, a second lifecycle owner, or a new dependency.

## Stop Conditions

Stop if exact claim arbitration cannot remain inside the existing local filesystem/process seam, if Orbit/Venus source must change, or if completion would interrupt live Sessions.
close_reason: Accepted source 871c9f639e519c7e3201fa5d9755d0a77a4cb0df proves rejected-Ready cleanup without post-Ready signal fallback.

title: Include generated managed behavior in Eon runtime generation identity
description:
## Contract routing

Harden the accepted EON-C11 runtime-generation contract and preserve EON-C9. The local launcher is the consumer; a build changes generated managed-shell adapters or the private Session command projection; the resulting Eon build must have a different stable generation identity so a bare launch cannot attach a supervisor with older managed behavior. This is a defect correction, not a new command, configuration field, protocol value, compatibility window, or distribution promise.

## Why

The generation digest covers Rust, Cargo, EONW, and component-manifest inputs but omits the Nix-owned generated shell adapters and private command projection. A flake-only runtime behavior fix can therefore retain the previous identity, attach the old supervisor, and give new panes its captured old Session environment.

Impact: HIGH. Effort: M. Implementation risk: MEDIUM. Confidence: HIGH.

## Evidence

- `crates/eon/src/main.rs:35-47`: `current_generation()` does not cover `flake.nix` or an equivalent managed-runtime projection identity.
- `flake.nix:228-479`: Nix generates runtime-visible native shell adapters.
- `flake.nix:537-585`: Nix constructs the private Session command projection and injects it into Session PATH.
- `crates/eon/src/main.rs:1220-1245`: a same-generation launch attaches the existing supervisor.
- `crates/eon/src/main.rs:2019-2025`: new panes use the existing supervisor's captured managed-program inputs.
- `eon-audit-eon-managed-environment-hay` records the exact 1b8836e audit and reproduction analysis.

## Prerequisite and reference gate

- No implementation prerequisite. This Bead is the prerequisite for the two EON-C9 managed-environment corrections found by the audit.
- Before code, record the repository execution baseline and classify the EON-C11 and EON-C9 proof records plus the managed-environment and runtime-generation entries in `docs/REFERENCES.md`.
- Required evidence is current EON-C11 generation selection, the exact Nix-generated adapters/private-bin owner, `eon-pxn.4` acceptance evidence, and the closed managed-environment audit.
- Existing Eon sources define the mechanism. External terminal or shell references are comparison-only unless an observed failure requires them.
- No dependency or crate feature is expected. Stop for the crate gate and user approval before any manifest change.

## Scope

In scope:
- The stable input set owned by `current_generation()` and the minimum Nix/build wiring needed to cover generated managed-runtime behavior.
- Focused unit/build/process proof that a managed-projection-only change selects a new generation while the old one remains live.
- Current-state EON-C11 proof metadata, CHANGELOG, architecture wording, and README LOC only where required by the accepted fix.

Out of scope:
- Hashing profile paths, store paths, PIDs, socket names, package channels, mutable user configuration, or runtime state.
- A Nix evaluator at runtime, a second runtime manifest, a manager daemon, live handoff, automatic old-generation eviction, or wider compatibility.
- Changing EONW, Orbit, Venus, shell behavior, managed command names, defaults, or user configuration.
- Adding a new dependency or speculative distribution framework.

Platform classification: neutral contract with an isolated current Nix build input; no new macOS blocker. A future distributor must be able to provide an equivalent stable behavior identity without Nix-specific runtime state.

## Implementation notes

1. Add the smallest existing build/source input that completely covers the generated adapter and private-bin behavior. Prefer conservative source hashing over a second schema or runtime mechanism.
2. Keep one generation owner in `current_generation()`; build tooling may supply immutable inputs but must not reinterpret launch policy.
3. Preserve old live generations and exact attach/stop behavior. Only the identity of builds with materially different managed projections should need to change.
4. Add one A/B regression whose only observable input difference is generated managed behavior.
5. Advance the EON-C11 proof revision after the proof-bearing commit and refresh the installed runtime without stopping old supervisors or Sessions.

## Acceptance

- Two builds with unchanged Rust, protocol, and component manifest but different observable generated managed behavior report different generation identities.
- A live build A remains discoverable and usable; bare launch of build B selects a fresh B supervisor; a pane created under B observes the B marker rather than A's projection.
- Rebuilding the same accepted inputs yields the same generation identity.
- Identity and persistent records expose no Nix store/profile path or mutable user state.
- Existing exact attach, listing, stop, cleanup, workspace, and managed-environment tests retain their observable results.
- No new contract, dependency, protocol, component identity, or compatibility window is introduced.

## Verification

- One focused A/B build/process check should exit 0 and prove distinct generations plus old-work preservation and B-pane behavior.
- `cargo fmt --check`
- `cargo check --locked`
- `cargo test --locked`
- `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo run --locked -p eon-manifest -- components/eon-alpha-v1.json`
- `nix build --no-link --print-out-paths --no-update-lock-file path:.#default`
- `nix flake check --no-update-lock-file path:.`
- `git diff --check`
- Installed `eon versions` and active profile/store-path checks after the accepted proof commit.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if the cited code or EON-C11 ownership has drifted materially.
- Stop if complete coverage requires a new public manifest, protocol field, dependency, distribution promise, or duplicate generation owner.
- Stop if the candidate identity depends on a mutable path/state value or requires evaluating Nix at runtime.
- Stop if the A/B proof cannot distinguish the corrected build from an ambient PATH or already-running supervisor.
- Stop if the same verification failure repeats twice after a reasonable correction.

## Maintenance notes

The first sufficient shape is one additional immutable generation input consumed by the existing owner. Do not create a general build-fingerprint framework. `eon-5rp` remains responsible only for keeping extracted Rust production sources in the digest.

1. Do nothing: rejected because a flake-only runtime behavior change can reuse the old supervisor and its captured environment.
2. Hash the tracked `flake.nix` bytes in the existing `current_generation()` input list and include that file in the existing Nix Rust source fileset: selected. It is conservative but complete for the current sole Nix composition owner, stable across identical source, distribution-neutral as source bytes rather than a store identity, and requires no new mechanism.
3. Inject derivation/store paths or hashes through wrapper environment: rejected because it makes Nix resolution identity part of runtime policy and risks self/reference or channel-specific identity.
4. Add a build script, generated fingerprint file, second runtime manifest, or normalized managed-behavior schema: rejected as duplicate ownership and maintenance for behavior already centralized in one tracked flake.

Decision:
- Add `flake.nix` as one more immutable source input to the existing generation digest and to the package source fileset. Accept conservative invalidation by unrelated tracked flake edits: it preserves live work and is cheaper and safer than maintaining a partial projection. Revisit only if non-runtime flake churn measurably creates harmful generation accumulation or direct distribution activates an equivalent channel input.

Cheapest proof:
- Before the fix, build two disposable exact source trees differing only by one observable generated managed-adapter marker and show identical `eon versions` generation values. After the fix, repeat and require distinct values; rebuild an unchanged tree and require stability. Then keep generation A live, select B by bare launch, and prove A survives while a B pane observes B behavior.

Exit condition:
- Stop for user approval if complete coverage requires a public schema, dependency, build script, store/path identity, child change, or compatibility promise. None is currently required.
