title: Design and prove native macOS Eon distribution
description:
## Outcome and contract

Distribute the accepted full Eon component set through a native macOS boundary under EON-C7. This Bead owns delivery only: it consumes an already proved macOS runtime and does not implement Orbit, Venus, EonTerm, or full-Eon platform behavior.

Private Nova consumption of EonTerm is intentionally independent. Nova may consume exact private EonTerm packages through `eon-4is.6` before full Eon is signed, notarized, published, or available through Homebrew.

## Prerequisites and order

1. `eon-p93` approves graduation from Nix-only dogfood and selects the direct-distribution target and maintenance envelope.
2. `eon-ohh` proves the shared direct-release artifact, verification, upgrade, rollback, and removal foundation on Linux.
3. `eon-prove-full-eon-apple-silicon-macos-t8o` proves the canonical full Eon composition natively on Apple Silicon macOS.
4. This Bead packages the exact accepted manifest and child proofs without introducing another component graph.

The existing graph dependency on `eon-ohh` is retained. Full Eon composition is an additional real prerequisite. This remains P2 because runtime portability for Nova/EonTerm is the prioritized P1 path.

## Reference and tool gate

Required before code: current Apple signing, hardened runtime, entitlements, notarization, stapling, Gatekeeper, quarantine, application bundle and disk-image behavior; Homebrew Cask requirements; universal versus architecture-specific artifacts; exact runtime child proofs; canonical component manifest; active-work-safe upgrade policy; and credible release tooling. Record required credentials, secrets boundary, hosted/local cost, architecture support, dependency/tool footprint, local LOC, replacement cost, and failure recovery. Stop for user approval before selecting or adding a release tool.

Keep signing identity, notarization credentials, and release authority outside repository state. Use the same immutable artifacts, checksums, signatures, manifest, and version diagnostics across direct download and Cask. Do not make a website or package manager the artifact authority.

## Acceptance

1. The selected architecture set has one immutable Eon application artifact or disk image, checksum, signature, notarization ticket, and exact component manifest; Apple Silicon is the first candidate and Intel/universal support is explicit rather than implied.
2. Gatekeeper, quarantine, first launch, repeat launch, version diagnostics, active-work-safe upgrade, rollback where supported, and removal are verified on a clean macOS user account.
3. A Homebrew Cask installs and removes the exact same immutable artifact without rebuilding or changing the component graph.
4. Application identity, bundle layout, entitlements, privacy prompts, filesystem locations, logs, user data, and cleanup ownership are explicit. Uninstall preserves user data unless the user separately requests its exact removal.
5. Every Linux assumption that required an owned boundary or child fix is recorded with its owning proof. Runtime behavior is never inferred from packaging success.
6. Exact credentials/tool boundaries, artifact sizes, closure contents, commands, environments, costs, limitations, and rollback/removal results are recorded at an immutable release candidate.

## Scope

No runtime feature, child fix, second manifest, Nova package change, hidden Nix dependency, Intel/universal promise without proof, App Store distribution, auto-updater, or public release occurs implicitly. Do not simulate native distribution with a Linux-only package foundation.

title: Browse untracked tab directories through Yazi
description:
## Chosen contract and authorization
User approved option 2 (quick search first, Yazi browsing fallback) and requested documentation and implementation on 2026-09-07. This issue now owns that implementation, replacing its completed investigation-only scope.

Consumer: a person selecting the launch directory for a fresh or existing full-Eon tab. Quick search remains the default; Enter accepts one ranked directory, Esc opens Yazi without ending the picker, Ctrl+C cancels. Empty history remains a usable quick-search screen with the same visible Browse action. In Yazi, arrows/hjkl browse; Shift+Z opens built-in Zoxide search and only changes browser CWD; Enter explicitly uses the current folder; q/Q/Ctrl+C cancel. Files provide orientation but are not opened. Existing EON-C18 first/later/existing-tab cancellation, validation and cleanup remain intact.

## Ownership and scope
Eon owns mode transition, fixed picker configuration, one absolute directory result and existing tab lifecycle/validation. Zoxide owns ranking; fzf owns quick selection; packaged Yazi owns filesystem browsing. No child pins, protocol, Lua plugin, recursive Eon walker, new dependency, editor/file-opening integration, topology or running-session changes.

## Evidence and decision
Baseline: clean Eon edge 43d344a; Orbit pin 91999d79546422b49bdbc124166a65859d0bd872 and Venus pin e13970e90289d0d86f0adcbf350e4b9c1d5e5219 match latest accepted runtime source (later child commits are proof metadata).
Inspected Nova 29514faf4a252d581b1577b79aa74b325584c766 custom zoxide-editor plugin and keymap: Alt+Z commits workspace; built-in Shift+Z only navigates. Inspected packaged Yazi 26.5.6 aa526434f00bb44e2e902d9a4ac5f810da1018b9 keymap, zoxide plugin, args, quit, file-provider output, terminal writer and DDS state; Zoxide 0.9.9 9cdc6aa3740b4d8a9d62406c99e84c5de49645e9 query/util; fzf 0.73.1 ce4bef75954bebd87e0886435bcf8c6904328ab0 usage/walker mechanisms. Prior disposable PTY checks proved Yazi known-parent jump then untracked-child navigation, directory return and cancellation; fzf walker found untracked/hidden directories.
Chosen: use Zoxide ranked list and fzf expected-key output to distinguish Esc from cancellation without shell actions or parsing Zoxide score columns. Use Yazi native cwd output and TOML keymap, no copied Nova plugin. Preserve byte paths at final Eon validation. Yazi navigates requested directories and exposes hidden toggle/home/root/direct path; no Eon whole-tree scan or new latency guarantee.
Rejected: typed-path mini tabs miss discovery; custom walker duplicates Yazi; recursive fzf list lacks parent/child context; intercepting every failed quick query as Browse hides errors; shared normal Yazi keymap permits ambiguous confirmation and unwanted file opening.
acceptance_criteria: Focused red/green picker integration proves Enter/escaped Browse/Ctrl+C separation, empty history, browser confirmation/cancellation/failure and byte-preserving directory validation. Packaged PTY checks prove actual fzf expected-key output and Yazi controls with hostile ambient picker options. Refresh regular eon profile and observe one isolated installed native-Wayland sequence: browse into untracked directory, commit, create pane at chosen CWD, cancel later picker, preserve other live user Sessions. Record exact source/artifact/generation and phase. Update EON-C18, README, changelog, references and LOC.
close_reason: Implemented, documented, mechanically verified and dogfooded through the refreshed regular Eon profile.

title: Decide whether Eon needs an extension system
description:
Contract disposition:
This decision creates no compatibility surface or runtime contract. Eon remains configuration-first and has no general plugin system. If the user later chooses an extension system, approve and index a separate EON contract before implementation.

Current product direction:
Proceed in order: finish and dogfood the core Eon workspace; prove one Eon-owned semantic action registry and make the `eon` CLI its canonical human and agent projection; let one declarative Eon configuration schema and external programs consume those actions; then reconsider plugins only if real recurring needs remain unsolved. Human-readable output and deterministic `--json` output are views of the same action owner, not separate APIs. The action surface and its private local control transport are not a plugin ABI, and configuration must not become an accidental programming language.

Goal:
After eon-pxn proves the workspace, action surface, and declarative-profile boundary, decide whether built-in owner code, the action API, external commands, configuration, or child-owned extension systems are insufficient and a stable Eon extension boundary is justified.

Prerequisites:
- eon-pxn and its activated owner children prove and dogfood the Eon workspace, deterministic action surface, and bounded declarative profile.
- Dogfood records at least two concrete recurring extension cases from different workflows and routes each through the existing owners first.
- The user explicitly activates this decision work; it does not become an implementation frontier automatically.

Ownership:
Eon may own product orchestration, workspace metadata, semantic actions, one product configuration schema and apply policy, and, only if later approved, extension installation, grants, activation, and compatibility. Ratconfig owns reusable configuration editing while consuming the Eon-owned schema and model. Orbit remains plugin-free and owns PTYs, sessions, terminal state, and ORBS/ORBF. Venus owns native rendering and may render only host-defined declarative contributions. Helix and Yazi keep their own extension mechanisms.

Scope:
Research and decide only. Do not add a runtime, SDK, manifest format, extension host, marketplace, plugin API, child-protocol capability, or production code. Do not let external automation or extensions receive raw PTY or protocol frames, fabricate provider state, inject arbitrary UI trees, or bypass separately approved Orbit observation contracts.
design:
Decision ladder:
1. Continue core product work. First-party workspace, tab, pane, attention, graphics, mouse, accessibility, and presentation needs are not plugin evidence.
2. Prove one excellent Eon-owned semantic action registry and its canonical `eon` CLI in eon-pxn. The running supervisor alone owns live workspace and action state behind a private Eon local control endpoint. The CLI exposes stable semantic identities, context-sensitive available actions, typed arguments, structured results, unavailable-action reasons, cancellation, and bounded errors through human-readable output and deterministic `--json` output. It does not address child protocols directly, and begins explicitly versioned and experimental; no stable 1.0 or plugin compatibility promise is implied.
3. Prove one bounded declarative configuration system over the same owner-authored actions. It may describe workspace and launch profiles, keybindings, named action sequences, explicit environment and working-directory inputs, and accepted presentation choices. It has one Eon-owned schema and Ratconfig editing. It does not gain loops, mutable variables, asynchronous callbacks, arbitrary code, custom widget trees, raw terminal control, or a second state owner. External commands using the action surface are the escape hatch.
4. Reopen the plugin decision only when two recurring cases cannot be expressed safely by the first three rungs or a child-owned extension system.

Required comparison:
A. Keep built-ins plus child-owned extension mechanisms.
B. Use the canonical `eon` CLI and the same narrow action protocol from external tools or commands without Eon-owned extension discovery, installation, activation, hosting, SDK promises, or plugin compatibility.
C. Use schema-backed declarative Eon configuration over the action API.
D. Add a plugin system using one of the credible architectures below.

Plugin architecture candidates, only after dogfood earns them:
1. Out-of-process extension executables over the same bounded framed local action protocol. Their implementation language is private and unrestricted; Eon promises the protocol, not supported languages or SDKs. This is the preferred first candidate for trusted local extensions because it reuses the action owner, fits Eon process supervision and Nix-pinned executables, and isolates crashes. Process separation alone is not an authority boundary; ambient user authority and OS sandboxing remain explicit.
2. WebAssembly Components with WIT and a credible runtime only when demonstrated cases require portable untrusted distribution, default-deny capability imports, or resource isolation that the selected process boundary cannot provide. Multiple guest languages are not themselves a product requirement. Record runtime weight, build and startup cost, standards maturity, toolchains, Linux and macOS support, and removal cost.
3. An embedded language runtime only when the demonstrated cases require synchronous or high-frequency in-process callbacks that the external action protocol cannot satisfy. At that point compare no runtime with exact credible languages and require the selected runtime to remove a complete Eon responsibility. Do not choose a language for syntax taste, agent novelty, or programmable configuration alone.

Language and runtime disposition:
Zero, Roto, Steel, Lua, Luau, and other languages remain discovery inputs rather than standing candidates. Zero is useful comparison evidence for semantic graph inspection, checked edits, typed facts, explicit effects, and agent-facing diagnostics, but its current experimental compiled toolchain is not an Eon extension host, stable compatibility boundary, or security sandbox. Reconsider a named language only when a demonstrated extension case and exact current evidence make its runtime uniquely credible.

Native Rust dynamic-library plugins are not a default candidate because they couple compiler and ABI choices to the host and place extension failure in the Eon process. Reconsider them only if exact evidence makes that coupling advantageous.

Reference gate:
Begin with the demonstrated cases, the exact accepted eon-pxn action, CLI, and configuration contracts, and the exact owner mechanisms they consume. First test whether built-ins, child-owned extensions, `eon` CLI composition, bounded wait or events, configuration, or an ordinary external process solve each case. Inspect an out-of-process extension-host precedent only if Eon-owned installation and activation remain necessary. Inspect WebAssembly Components, WIT, and a selected runtime only for a demonstrated untrusted portable-code requirement. Inspect a named embedded language only for a demonstrated synchronous in-process requirement. Compare no new dependency, existing process and protocol facilities, release health, licenses, Linux and macOS support, dependency and compile weight, security posture, owned LOC, compatibility burden, and removal cost. Agent-authoring ergonomics are secondary to ownership, failure isolation, security, portability, and compatibility.

Security and lifecycle gate:
Default-deny filesystem, environment, process spawning, network, clipboard, secrets, raw terminal or protocol data, GPU, windows, webviews, and background execution. Separate read-only observation from mutation. Define memory, wall-time, queue, message, result, log, storage, concurrency, activation, cancellation, crash, restart, and shutdown bounds. An extension-host crash must not terminate Orbit or Venus, and safe mode must disable third-party extensions.

Distribution and compatibility gate:
Start with local or Nix-pinned immutable bundles only. Identity is publisher, name, version, API version, and content hash, never a Nix store path. Permissions match imported capabilities and re-prompt when expanded. Defer a marketplace, arbitrary panels, custom widget trees, remote installation, signing infrastructure, and a multi-language support promise. Define the selected API version policy and make no stable compatibility promise before an explicitly approved 1.0 API.

Stop conditions:
Stop with no plugin feature if built-ins, the action API, external commands, declarative configuration, or child-owned plugins cover the demonstrated needs. Stop if the design needs Orbit plugins, raw ORBS/ORBF access, duplicated terminal or provider state, speculative capability negotiation, ambient authority presented as sandboxing, or a marketplace before local extensions prove value. Stop for explicit user choice before creating a contract or implementation bead.
acceptance_criteria:
1. eon-pxn and its activated owner children prove the core workspace, deterministic action surface, and bounded declarative-profile boundary before this decision starts.
2. Dogfood supplies at least two independent recurring extension cases and explains why built-in owner code, the action API, external commands, declarative configuration, and child-owned plugins do not solve them. First-party tabs, panes, overlays, status items, graphics, mouse behavior, accessibility, and presentation do not count as extension demand.
3. The record distinguishes the Eon-owned action registry and canonical CLI from a plugin system: actions expose semantic state and behavior through human-readable and deterministic structured projections, while extension discovery, installation, activation, hosting, grants, SDK promises, and compatibility remain absent unless explicitly approved. The running supervisor is the sole live action-state owner, and the CLI or external clients never bypass it by speaking child protocols directly.
4. The configuration candidate has one Eon-owned schema and apply policy, is edited through Ratconfig, consumes accepted semantic actions, and contains no arbitrary executable language, loops, mutable callbacks, custom widget trees, raw terminal control, or duplicate state.
5. The comparison grades continuing with built-ins, API plus external tools, declarative configuration, and a plugin system against product value, human and agent usability, architecture, security, portability, dependency cost, compatibility burden, and removal cost.
6. If plugins remain justified, the reference and crate or tool gates start with out-of-process executable extensions over the accepted Eon action protocol. They evaluate WebAssembly Components only for demonstrated portable untrusted-code or isolation needs, and a named embedded runtime only for demonstrated synchronous or high-frequency in-process needs that the external protocol cannot meet. They compare no new dependency and record why Zero or any other language is or is not credible at its exact current revision. Eon makes no supported-language, SDK, or multi-language promise merely because executable or Wasm boundaries permit several implementations.
7. The decision names one owner for identity, installation, activation, grants, actions, UI contributions, state, failures, and compatibility while preserving Orbit, Venus, Ratconfig, Helix, and Yazi ownership.
8. A threat model and capability table cover filesystem, environment, process, network, clipboard, secrets, terminal observation, UI, storage, and background work with deny-by-default behavior. Process separation is not claimed as authority isolation without an OS sandbox.
9. Resource, lifecycle, crash-isolation, safe-mode, Linux and macOS, distribution, upgrade, removal, and API-version policies are explicit and falsifiable.
10. Any proposed plugin proof contains exactly the two demonstrated first-party extensions and checks useful behavior, permission denial, runaway execution, extension crash, incompatible API version, and clean removal.
11. The record estimates owned LOC, dependency weight, compile and runtime cost, maintenance, and permanent compatibility cost and names evidence that would reverse the recommendation.
12. The user explicitly chooses keep built-ins and the CLI/action API only, add declarative configuration only, use a narrow out-of-process extension contract, adopt WebAssembly Components for a demonstrated portable untrusted-code or isolation requirement, adopt a named embedded runtime for a demonstrated in-process requirement, reject plugins, or defer.
13. Closure creates no runtime code, dependency, manifest, protocol change, marketplace, SDK, or compatibility promise.
notes:
User-approved planning direction on 2026-08-08: sequence core product work, a narrow high-quality action API, schema-backed declarative configuration, and only then a plugin decision if dogfood still demonstrates unmet needs.

Current judgment:
- Continue core workspace work: A for the present frontier.
- One Eon-owned semantic action registry with the canonical `eon` CLI for humans and agents: A+, the preferred control and extensibility backbone.
- Bounded declarative configuration and ordinary external programs consuming the same actions: A, the preferred customization and automation layers.
- General plugin system: D at the current product stage, with an A- ceiling only after concrete demand and successful ownership, security, lifecycle, portability, and compatibility gates.

If plugins are later earned, out-of-process executables over the accepted action protocol are the preferred first candidate for trusted local extensions. Their language remains a private implementation detail rather than an Eon support promise. WebAssembly Components are conditional on demonstrated untrusted portable-code or isolation requirements. An embedded runtime is conditional on demonstrated synchronous in-process requirements that external actions cannot meet. No architecture, SDK, supported guest language, or durable second language is selected by this planning decision.

Priority P4 remains intentional. This work follows the eon-pxn workspace and action proof rather than competing with Orbit, Venus, or the first Eon workspace frontier.

Feature-horizon boundary: eon-pxn owns bounded native horizontal tabs, visual vertical accordion panes, semantic actions, and declarative workspace or profile pressure as first-party product architecture. Generic overlays, floating terminal popups, arbitrary split trees, fixed status items, semantic mouse routing, accessibility focus, and graphics remain first-party owner concerns rather than plugin evidence.

Planning effort M; implementation risk HIGH because every published capability becomes a security and compatibility surface. Confidence HIGH in API-first and configuration-first sequencing, HIGH in deferring plugins, and LOW that an embedded runtime is justified before concrete cases exist.

First-principles language disposition approved on 2026-08-08:
- Eon needs one semantic action owner and canonical CLI, not an Eon-specific plugin language.
- Zero is retained as high-value comparison evidence for agent-queryable semantic interfaces, not selected as a dependency or extension runtime.
- Syntax elegance, static typing, and single-language ecosystem preferences do not outrank child ownership, crash isolation, security, portability, protocol stability, and removal cost.
- A language or runtime becomes credible only when dogfood supplies a case that the CLI, external actions, configuration, and child-owned mechanisms cannot solve.

title: Deliver long, pixel-smooth kinetic Eon scrollback
description:
## Chosen product contract

Deliver useful retained terminal history and responsive native-Wayland scrolling without moving terminal authority out of Orbit or adding a second scheduling/rendering architecture.

Consumer: one installed Eon/EonTerm user on supported x86_64 Linux native Wayland.
Trigger: primary-screen history owns scrolling and the user moves a precision/continuous surface or discrete wheel.
Result: Orbit retains a measured useful byte budget and applies bounded signed whole-row movement atomically; Venus presents direct fractional pixels, bounded release momentum only when the native phase supports it, three rows per discrete logical step, and compositor-paced FIFO redraw; Eon composes exact accepted child revisions and records installed dogfood.
Important failures: terminal-owned input keeps its canonical physical routing and receives no synthetic momentum; all motion is interruptible; history edges stop firmly; background output never produces stale/invented rows; profile refresh preserves live Sessions.

When measured safe choices are otherwise equivalent, prefer the more responsive/lively behavior while preserving 1:1 low-speed precision, exact distance, bounded stopping, routing, and authority.

## Owner beads and sequence

This epic is a planning container and is never claimed for implementation.

1. Finish the existing active Eon Sessions lifecycle frontier.
2. Eon Sessions `orb-orbit-history-byte-budget-ykn`: measure and set the Orbit-owned history byte budget.
3. Eon Sessions `orb-orbit-signed-scroll-batch-x12`: extend `ORB-C8` and the next canonical ORBS version with one atomic bounded signed history commit.
4. Eon Desktop `ven-venus-kinetic-touchpad-scroll-5sl`: revise `VEN-C7` for fractional presentation, native input interpretation, minimal elapsed-time physics, batching, pacing, and honest metrics.
5. Eon `eon-kinetic-scrollback-bjs.1`: pin exact accepted children, refresh the active Nix profile without restarting live Sessions, and dogfood the installed candidate.
6. After that first installed dogfood, Eon Desktop `ven-decide-winit-scroll-gestures-mfz` records the explicit choice to keep pinned winit, backport narrowly, adopt a stable release, or—only with user approval—use an exact unreleased revision. It does not block owner implementation or the first candidate, but it precedes final epic closure.

Cross-repository relationships are recorded by exact IDs rather than duplicated Beads. The two Orbit beads share a workflow prerequisite but no false technical dependency; Eon Sessions still implements only one active frontier at a time.

## Reference decision

Inspected 2026-08-24:

- Orbit `bad068a775140a1a4c4a157a0b9b64fba46f8202` and pinned Ghostty `a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083`: current `max_scrollback: 1_000` is bytes, not rows; existing `ORB-C8` already owns authoritative adjacent preview, routing, viewport movement, and frames.
- Venus `082ecb7e9e2a8dde009db28e481a68bee2d3ace6`: current path truncates native movement to rows and may amplify one event into repeated requests/frames; existing winit, wgpu FIFO, glyphon, and event loop remain the chosen owners.
- Pinned winit 0.30.13 fork `fb45fbf901fbe70cc9a877b5d651d0b60c206b08`: Wayland exposes line versus pixel deltas and phases but discards axis source, native event time, and useful device identity. Core policy is therefore based only on observable delta/phase.
- Winit master `874a1e31f194d11313c1ac133b28037b99db3e19` has unreleased hold gestures and newer high-resolution wheel support but still lacks source/time/device guarantees. Defer selection until hardware dogfood identifies whether those capabilities matter.
- Wayland pointer semantics: https://wayland.app/protocols/wayland
- GTK's current frame-clock and elapsed-time kinetic model, Kitty's pixel/momentum behavior, winit redraw/presentation notification, WGPU FIFO latency, libinput scrolling, Ghostty history semantics, and Alacritty's useful-history/wheel defaults are routed in the owner beads.

Adopt: 16 MiB as a measured starting hypothesis; one-row authoritative preview as the architecture ceiling; one signed batch in flight; fractional rendering; phase-complete precision momentum; direct discrete wheels; actual elapsed-time decay; compositor callbacks; existing glyphon first; honest event-delivery-to-submit metrics.

Reject for the first slice: rows as the history unit, nominal fixed 60 Hz timers, fixed per-frame decay, device/source guesses, synthetic discrete-wheel inertia, velocity stacking, bounce, one frame per row, multi-row overscan, custom renderer/shader, refresh discovery, actual-presentation protocols, public tuning, new mouse bindings, worker threads, physics dependencies, or unreleased-winit adoption before dogfood.

## Epic acceptance

1. Both Orbit beads and the Venus bead close with exact accepted revisions, contract/docs alignment, focused owner proof, and full affected shared-protocol surfaces.
2. `eon-kinetic-scrollback-bjs.1` proves the exact installed component graph and profile artifact, retains live Sessions during refresh, and records real supported-Wayland hardware behavior across the agreed gesture, wheel, edge, live-output, routing, cancellation, resize, reconnect, and lifecycle cases.
3. The accepted metrics demonstrate control and identify the actual bottleneck: no lost distance, stale/invented rows, runaway tail, bounce, unbounded queue, terminal-routing regression, or misleading physical-input/visible-presentation claim.
4. Available 60 Hz and 120+ Hz surfaces are observed without promising a fixed cadence. If required hardware is unavailable, the proof records that gap rather than inferring it.
5. After first installed dogfood, `ven-decide-winit-scroll-gestures-mfz` records the user's explicit source decision. Any selected dependency change receives its own authorization and proof; “keep pinned” is a valid complete decision.
6. The user accepts the installed scroll length, sensitivity, smoothness, acceleration, stopping distance, and interruption behavior.

## Scope and stop conditions

In scope: the four owner slices above, exact composition, installed proof, and the post-dogfood winit decision.

Out of scope: scrollbar/search UI, persistent history, compression lifecycle, multi-row overscan, terminal cells owned by Venus, renderer replacement, public tuning/configuration, new mouse-button gestures, momentum inside terminal applications, display-refresh guarantees, X11/Xwayland/macOS, additional architectures, or init/service-manager work.

Stop and return to the user if the one-row preview is insufficient; a new dependency/thread/timer/renderer/public configuration appears necessary; protocol work expands beyond one bounded commit and atomic response; real hardware cannot be handled from existing observable events; per-device policy becomes necessary; or measurement cannot identify a bounded existing-owner fix.

title: Accept installed Eon kinetic scrollback
description:
## Outcome and contract routing

Compose the exact accepted Orbit and Venus kinetic-scrollback revisions into Eon and record one installed native-Wayland acceptance. This refreshes the proofs for `EON-C1` through `EON-C4`; it adds no Eon-owned scrolling, input, rendering, or terminal state.

Consumer: one installed Eon/EonTerm user on supported x86_64 Linux native Wayland.
Trigger: the accepted child revisions are available and Eon selects them in its canonical component graph.
Result: the Nix profile resolves to the just-built exact component set, existing live Sessions are preserved until the user restarts them, and a fresh installed surface exposes Orbit-owned useful history plus Venus-owned direct pixel scrolling, bounded kinetic release, discrete-wheel behavior, and compositor-paced presentation.
Important failures: incompatible pins/builds fail before profile activation; profile refresh does not restart a live supervisor; dogfood must not claim physical-input-to-screen timing or guaranteed display cadence unavailable from the accepted APIs.

## Prerequisites and references

Accepted child work:

- Eon Sessions `orb-orbit-history-byte-budget-ykn`: measured retained-history byte budget.
- Eon Sessions `orb-orbit-signed-scroll-batch-x12`: accepted canonical ORBS v7 bounded signed history commit.
- Eon Desktop `ven-venus-kinetic-touchpad-scroll-5sl`: exact protocol consumer, fractional renderer, input policy, physics, pacing, and instrumentation.

Accepted rollout source `b44d968e38474fc5b75a41bcde2ad750da0d1e3e` pins Orbit `baf8aa28dcaa50484cd221aa7730defedc2356bb` with ORBS v7 and Venus `f13dc7ac2e9a24c5cff5bb7e618436783ec76dbf`.

The post-dogfood winit decision `ven-decide-winit-scroll-gestures-mfz` is deliberately non-blocking. Run it after this installed runtime is dogfooded; do not expand the first slice to an unreleased dependency beforehand.

## Acceptance

1. The canonical manifest, lock identities, Venus protocol import, and Nix composition name the exact accepted Orbit and Venus revisions with no compatibility probe, adapter, duplicate schema, or copied child mechanism.
2. Full affected Rust and Nix surfaces pass because the work crosses the shared ORBS protocol and installed UI. Refresh the active `eon` profile from the working tree and verify it resolves to the resulting store artifact.
3. Preserve running supervisors and Sessions during profile refresh. With explicit user authorization to stop/restart or after natural closure, launch one fresh installed Eon/EonTerm surface for outermost proof.
4. Installed dogfood covers: retained-history usefulness; slow sub-row precision; weak and strong releases; detented and rapid wheels; history edges; background PTY output; semantic-key live return; selection and mouse buttons; cursor/focus/occlusion loss; resize; pane/session changes; reconnect; terminal mouse tracking; and repeated launch/close lifecycle.
5. On available 60 Hz and 120+ Hz displays, retain the child metrics for event-delivery-to-redraw/present-submit, redraw cadence/missed callbacks, requested/applied distance, Orbit batch/frame time, renderer preparation/submission, coalescing, fling duration, and stopping distance. Report unavailable hardware honestly and make no refresh-rate guarantee.
6. The user accepts that movement is exact, responsive, controllable, and sufficiently long-lived, with no lost distance, stale/invented rows, runaway tail, bounce, queue-pressure notice, terminal-routing regression, or lifecycle regression.
7. `docs/CONTRACTS.md`, component records, changelog, README LOC scorecard, exact installed artifact, and Beads proof all agree at the same revisions.

## Scope boundary and stop conditions

In scope: exact child pinning, canonical composition, Eon and EonTerm profile refresh, exact Eonova downstream pin/profile refresh, installed proof, and user acceptance.

Out of scope: Eon-owned scroll policy or state, winit selection, renderer/protocol redesign, public tuning, new platform support, init/service-manager work, or any child fix copied into Eon.

Stop and return to the user if a child contract is not accepted, the profile cannot resolve the exact built artifact, installed behavior contradicts child proof, live Sessions would need automatic interruption, or dogfood reaches a recorded child stop condition.

title: Initialize Orbit with the Eon vivid ANSI palette
description:
## Outcome and contract

Consumer: a local user opening a new full Eon or EonTerm Session.

Trigger: Eon starts a new Orbit process for that Session.

Result: Eon supplies one exact approved 16-color sRGB ANSI table through a bounded versioned component launch input. Orbit validates it, applies it as the authoritative default palette before processing PTY output, and emits the resulting exact values through existing ORBS frames. Full Eon and EonTerm use the same table. Terminal programs may still override colors through normal OSC semantics.

Important failures: malformed or missing required Eon input fails before the PTY child starts; partial tables are rejected; an Orbit process started outside Eon keeps its existing libghostty defaults; current live Sessions are not recolored or restarted. Direct RGB and palette indices 16 through 255 remain unchanged. OSC 4 overrides remain program-owned, and OSC 104 resets to the Eon-supplied defaults rather than bare libghostty values.

Ownership: Eon is the sole owner of the product default table and component launch policy. Orbit remains the sole terminal-state owner and applies the accepted default through libghostty. Venus remains an exact ORBS consumer and gains no palette setting, rewrite, saturation transform, or renderer change.

Contract routing: harden EON-C1, EON-C3, EON-C4, and EON-C12; change or add an Eon user-visible default contract only after explicit user approval. The producer work must preserve ORB-C1, harden ORB-C2 and ORB-C6, and define the new Orbit launch input before code. Existing ORBS values already carry the complete palette, so no ORBS version or VEN contract change is proposed.

## Why

The P1 Venus issue ven-render-vivid-terminal-colors-2ap proved that YZX Anima indexed colors are muted before Venus: bright indices 10, 14, 12, and 13 arrive as #b9ca4a, #70c0b1, #7aa6da, and #c397d8, while generic direct RGB #00ff88 remains exact. The Venus renderer is not the owner, but the user-visible product defect remains. Without a correct-owner Eon issue, closing the Venus investigation loses the chosen vivid-color outcome.

Impact: HIGH. Common Zellij and Anima indexed output uses the default palette.
Effort: M across one producer-first Orbit slice and one Eon integration slice.
Risk: MED because startup validation and terminal palette reset semantics cross the component boundary.
Confidence: HIGH in ownership and mechanism; the exact 16-color table still requires explicit user acceptance.

## Evidence

- Eon crates/eon/src/main.rs:1596-1635 has one Orbit process and argv owner. It currently sends only serve, socket, separator, and child argv.
- Eon docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:101 assigns component launch policy to the Eon runtime and excludes terminal state.
- Orbit src/main.rs:180-228 accepts only socket and child command, then constructs libghostty with columns, rows, and scrollback.
- libghostty-vt 0.2.1 terminal.rs:158-224 and :710-725 exposes default_color_palette and set_default_color_palette for embedder-owned defaults. It preserves OSC overrides and makes later resets return to the supplied default.
- libghostty-vt 0.2.1 style.rs:225-330 provides the existing 256-entry Palette, base-index setters, and built-in defaults. No new parser crate or palette type is needed.
- Orbit src/presentation.rs:147-153 already emits the effective complete 256-color palette through ORBS.
- eon-eonterm-presentation-e4f is not a duplicate: it routes fonts, geometry, line height, and opacity to Venus and explicitly excludes terminal palette authority.
- No existing Eon or Orbit Bead mentions palette initialization.

Exact inspected identities: Eon a701d55beaf4127c9ff4d1341214b1ebd82221ba; Orbit e60554623d2ad1e238fac84d0f8f49be0e81e522; Venus investigation at eon-desktop b18d5c34f794fd4e3c34beb64952a767c588db41; Ghostty a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083 through libghostty-vt 0.2.1; Nova Bar d659fdf5ae0b4013aacaf31399e2bab064654320; packaged Anima d22d091d427af0be307056c65e475802b602d386.

## Minimum shape

1. Before implementation, capture the clean Ghostty palette and the user-approved vivid candidate beside Nova direct colors and the Anima/Zellij indexed corpus. Obtain explicit approval for all 16 RGB entries and whether foreground/background remain unchanged.
2. Create and prove a separate Orbit producer issue first. Define one bounded versioned launch value for exactly 16 RGB entries; reject partial or trailing input before PTY creation. Add no config framework or compatibility window.
3. In Orbit, start from the existing libghostty 256-color default, replace indices 0 through 15 with the supplied table, and call set_default_color_palette before the owner loop processes PTY bytes. Do not synthesize OSC, inject shell output, or change ORBS.
4. Prove initial frames, detach and reattach, OSC 4 override, per-index and full OSC 104 reset, direct RGB, and default standalone Orbit behavior.
5. After the exact Orbit proof is accepted, add the fixed approved table to the existing Eon Orbit-command owner and pass the exact child input for workspace and EonTerm launches. Add no user setting in this first slice.
6. Prove the composed installed artifact, update accepted contract metadata after proof-bearing commits, and refresh the Eon profile without stopping live supervisors or Sessions.

## Scope

In scope:
- One fixed Eon product-default ANSI 16-color table.
- Existing Eon Orbit launch composition and focused argv/process tests.
- A producer-first Orbit launch-input parser and direct existing libghostty palette setter.
- Contract, component-identity, current-state documentation, changelog, and LOC updates required by accepted runtime behavior.
- Native Linux dogfood in full Eon and EonTerm/Eonova with Zellij and YZX Anima Game of Life.

Out of scope:
- Venus source, renderer color transforms, saturation boosting, shaders, color management, or a Venus palette setting.
- A user-editable palette, theme registry, dark/light switching, live reload, per-pane colors, foreground/background changes without explicit approval, or Nova theme ownership.
- Replacing or forking libghostty, adding a dependency, changing ORBS, changing terminal direct RGB, or regenerating indices 16 through 255.
- Recoloring an existing Orbit process or restarting live Sessions.

## Reference classification

Required before code: this complete Bead; closed Venus issue ven-render-vivid-terminal-colors-2ap and its exact capture comments; current Eon launch owner and EON-C1/C3/C4/C12; current Orbit CLI, ORB-C1/C2/C6, palette extraction, lifecycle tests, and libghostty-vt 0.2.1 palette API; Ghostty a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083; Nova Bar d659fdf5ae0b4013aacaf31399e2bab064654320; packaged Anima d22d091d427af0be307056c65e475802b602d386.

Comparison only: a clean standalone Ghostty native capture and the users configured Ghostty capture. They inform exact palette choice but do not transfer Ghostty configuration or renderer ownership.

Rejected: Venus palette replacement, global saturation curves, synthetic OSC prelude, shell startup escapes, environment-variable-per-color, a general theme schema, Mars configuration import, source copying, and a new dependency.

## Acceptance

1. The user approves one exact complete 16-color sRGB table before contract or source edits. The proof records the compared clean Ghostty, configured Ghostty, Nova, and current libghostty values without claiming they are identical.
2. Eon owns one fixed table and passes one bounded versioned value to every newly started full Eon and EonTerm Orbit process. No second table or consumer reconstruction exists.
3. Orbit rejects malformed, incomplete, duplicate, or trailing palette input before PTY spawn and reports one bounded launch failure. Omitting the option outside Eon preserves the built-in default.
4. The first ORBS frame contains the exact approved table. Detach and reattach preserve it without changing terminal or process identity.
5. OSC 4 overrides only named indices; OSC 104 for one or all indices returns to the Eon table. Direct RGB and indices 16 through 255 remain exact.
6. Venus receives and renders the resulting existing ORBS values without source or contract changes.
7. Native full Eon and EonTerm/Eonova dogfood shows accepted vivid Zellij and YZX Anima colors beside unchanged Nova direct RGB. Existing live generations remain untouched and report restart as required.
8. Orbit is proved and published first; Eon then pins that exact accepted revision, updates component identity and contract proof, builds the package, refreshes the profile, and runs the locked checks.

## Verification

Orbit producer:
- cargo fmt --all --check
- cargo check --locked --workspace
- cargo test --locked --workspace
- cargo run --locked --quiet -p orbit-governance -- .
- cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
- git diff --check

Eon consumer:
- cargo test --locked -p eon orbit_uses_configured_argv_only_for_default_sessions
- cargo fmt --all --check
- cargo check --locked --workspace
- cargo test --locked --workspace
- cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
- cargo run --locked -p eon-manifest -- components/eon-alpha-v3.json
- nix build --no-link --print-out-paths --no-update-lock-file path:.#default
- nix flake check --no-build --no-update-lock-file path:.
- git diff --check

Record exact ORBS captures before and after OSC override/reset plus the installed native comparison. Success means exact bytes and accepted visual output, not merely compilation.

## Stop conditions

- Stop for explicit user approval before assigning or changing EON or ORB contract IDs and before fixing the 16-color table.
- Stop before Eon code until a separate Orbit producer issue is created, approved, proved, committed, and published at an exact revision.
- Stop if another active frontier owns the Eon launch path or Orbit CLI/terminal owner.
- Stop if the existing libghostty setter does not preserve OSC override and reset semantics under focused proof.
- Stop if the change requires an ORBS revision, libghostty fork, dependency, theme framework, public configuration, live Session mutation, or Venus workaround.

## Maintenance notes

Keep this separate from eon-eonterm-presentation-e4f so palette authority does not block independent Venus font and window settings. Reconcile it before activating the Eonova bridge acceptance or Nova cutover. The removal path is one Eon table, one component launch field, and one Orbit application path.

title: Define Eon as a Linux Wayland product
description:
Contract: revise EON-C7. Consumer: Eon users, release work, and child repositories. Trigger: platform, desktop-backend, or distribution decisions. Result: Eon supports Linux on native Wayland; each channel names the Linux architectures it actually proves. X11, Xwayland, and macOS are outside the product contract. Preserve platform-neutral wire formats and state where they remain the natural owner, without preserving a portability promise or parallel backend. Important failures: public docs, policy, and release design must not claim macOS or X11 support; child implementations must not be changed from this owner-only slice. Repository-local policy names Linux/Wayland as the sole platform and generated AGENTS.md matches it. The reference route records the adopted foot/Monstar mechanism and rejected cross-platform scope. README LOC is exact. No runtime, component manifest, child repository, or live Session changes occur.

title: Make Eon's private Session PATH resolve managed commands
description:
## Contract routing

Harden accepted EON-C9 without changing its command surface. A local Eon Session is the consumer; the configured/default argv names `eon-nu`, `eon-bash`, `eon-zsh`, or `eon-fish`; the package-private Session PATH must resolve that stable prefixed command to Eon's pinned managed dispatcher without relying on an ambient profile PATH. Missing packaged artifacts must still fail explicitly. Preserve EON-C11 generation selection.

## Why

The default is `eon-nu`, but the only PATH segment Eon guarantees to Sessions contains unprefixed private aliases. Direct package, Nix app, or composition launches can therefore fail before a shell starts; an installed profile in ambient PATH merely hides the defect.

Impact: HIGH. Effort: S. Implementation risk: LOW. Confidence: HIGH.

## Evidence

- `crates/eon/src/main.rs:951-959`: the default shell argv is `command = ["eon-nu"]`.
- `crates/eon/src/main.rs:1797-1805`: Session startup prepends only the private Session bin before executing the configured argv.
- `flake.nix:544-550`: `$out/bin` exposes `eon-*`, while `$out/libexec/eon/bin` exposes only unprefixed names.
- `flake.nix:584`: only `$out/libexec/eon/bin` is injected as the Session PATH prefix.
- `eon-audit-eon-managed-environment-hay`: exact artifact `/nix/store/h7vvb4lrxnyr23lzglclmf02ajwrk2ar-eon-0.1.0` failed to launch `eon-nu` with only the private PATH, while `nu --version` succeeded.

## Prerequisite and reference gate

- Blocked by `eon-generated-runtime-identity-h4g`; the flake-only correction must select a fresh supervisor after a profile update.
- Before code, record the execution baseline and read the complete closed audit, current EON-C9/EON-C11 proofs, the private-bin construction, and the managed-command dispatch tests.
- `docs/REFERENCES.md` evidence for the four native shells is comparison-only here; this fix changes name resolution, not shell startup semantics.
- No dependency or crate feature is expected. Stop for the crate gate and user approval before any manifest change.

## Scope

In scope:
- `flake.nix` private Session-bin projection for the four existing prefixed managed shell commands.
- The cheapest package-level regression that launches the exact packaged Orbit boundary with a private-only PATH.
- Current-state EON-C9 proof metadata, CHANGELOG, and README LOC where required by the accepted fix.

Out of scope:
- Changing the default shell, command names, public `$out/bin` behavior, unprefixed private aliases, PATH precedence, shell configuration, integration toggles, or argv semantics.
- Adding wrappers when the existing dispatcher/symlink pattern is sufficient.
- Changing Orbit, Venus, EONW, component pins, user PATH, or distribution policy.
- Adding dependencies or a shell framework.

Platform classification: neutral command contract with isolated current Nix packaging proof; no new macOS blocker.

## Implementation notes

1. Reuse the existing package-owned managed dispatcher and symlink projection; add the stable prefixed names to the private bin while preserving unprefixed aliases.
2. Add the failing package-boundary check first. Clear ambient PATH so it cannot mask the result.
3. Prove all four prefixed commands resolve to their pinned packaged shells; one parameterized check is sufficient.
4. Advance EON-C9 proof metadata after the proof-bearing commit and refresh the installed runtime without stopping older generations.

## Acceptance

- With HOME isolated and PATH containing only the exact package's private Session bin, `eon-nu --version`, `eon-bash --version`, `eon-zsh --version`, and `eon-fish --version` resolve and report their pinned package identities.
- The default `command = ["eon-nu"]` launches through exact packaged Orbit without any ambient profile bin.
- Unprefixed private aliases and public prefixed commands retain their current behavior.
- PATH ordering, managed environment filtering, user configuration, integration toggles, argv forwarding, and explicit missing-artifact failures remain unchanged.
- No new contract, dependency, wrapper layer, or public command is introduced.

## Verification

- The isolated exact-package Orbit/private-PATH regression should exit 0 for all four prefixed shell commands and fail before the fix.
- `cargo fmt --check`
- `cargo check --locked`
- `cargo test --locked`
- `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo run --locked -p eon-manifest -- components/eon-alpha-v1.json`
- `nix build --no-link --print-out-paths --no-update-lock-file path:.#default`
- `nix flake check --no-update-lock-file path:.`
- `git diff --check`
- Installed profile and `eon versions` checks after the accepted proof commit.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if the cited command/PATH ownership has drifted materially.
- Stop if the fix requires changing the accepted EON-C9 command surface, default, PATH precedence, or another repository.
- Stop if a test uses ambient profile resolution or bypasses Orbit and therefore cannot falsify the reported failure.
- Stop before adding a dependency, wrapper framework, protocol change, or compatibility path.
- Stop if the same verification failure repeats twice after a reasonable correction.

## Maintenance notes

The existing private-bin projection is the correct owner. Four additional symlink names are preferable to changing the default to an unprefixed implementation detail or teaching runtime code a second resolution rule.

title: Decide whether Eon earns a durable native semantic editor
description:
## Contract Routing

This is the product decision gate for a possible Eon-native durable semantic editor engine. It changes no product contract and authorizes no implementation, dependency, repository, protocol, or Helix removal. EON-C4 currently preserves Helix as the sole owner of editing, language integration, and editor state. A positive decision requires explicit user approval, an updated ownership architecture, and new or revised indexed EON and owner-repository contracts before code.

User constraint recorded 2026-08-12: if Eon adopts its own editor engine, it must provide Helix-like modal editing and preserve most Helix default keybindings regardless of whether it reuses `helix-core`. `eon-specify-helix-modal-semantics-3kl` and `eon-preserve-helix-keybindings-uca` make that requirement falsifiable.

## Why

A native editor is justified only if it unlocks a user-visible contract that opaque terminal-hosted Helix cannot supply: authoritative addressable documents and revisions, durable unsaved editor state, transient Venus attachment, semantic native presentation, and explicit human/agent edit-conflict boundaries. Native appearance, fewer visible processes, code ownership preference, or the existence of reusable Helix crates are insufficient.

The important question is not “Can Eon render text?” It is whether Eon can earn the permanent editor-feature, language-support, compatibility, security, durability, and maintenance burden while remaining more valuable than Helix running inside an Orbit Session.

## Current Evidence

Repository evidence:

- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:16` assigns editing, language integration, and editor state to Helix; `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:69` forbids Eon from implementing editor behavior under the accepted architecture.
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md:18` proves EON-C4's no-duplicate-child-state boundary. `README.md:249` exposes managed Helix as `eon-hx`.
- Orbit already proves a real PTY plus authoritative terminal state and complete structured attachment revisions; this does not expose Helix documents, selections, undo, diagnostics, or semantic commands.
- Venus already consumes host-authored snapshots while remaining transient. A future editor projection must preserve that ownership lesson without reusing the terminal grid as an editor schema.

Exact Helix evidence:

- Official Helix `079a789e8cb08ead67f19e1971a1b7438b37354b` (2026-07-23), MPL-2.0.
- `docs/architecture.md` describes `helix-core` as functional Rope, Selection, Transaction, and Syntax primitives, but says `helix-view` is currently tied to the terminal UI.
- `helix-term/src/keymap/default.rs` owns the default Normal, Select, and Insert tries. `helix-term/src/commands.rs` is 7,228 lines and owns substantial mappable-command behavior. Reusing `helix-core` alone therefore does not preserve Helix modal behavior or keybindings.
- `helix-core` is a credible candidate mechanism; `helix-view` and `helix-term` are not an accepted native-frontend seam at this revision.
- Recheck upstream issue #5555, issue #312, and PR #13468 at decision time for an accepted command/view/client split; their observed open work is discovery, not a supported contract.

External architecture evidence:

- CodeMirror 6 System Guide, https://codemirror.net/docs/guide/: accept immutable state and transaction lessons; reject its browser and extension architecture as an Eon requirement.
- Neovim UI protocol, https://neovim.io/doc/user/api-ui-events/: external clients are viable, but its terminal-like grid and multigrid model are a semantic ceiling Eon should not copy for a native editor.
- Kakoune client/server design, https://kakoune.org/why-kakoune/why-kakoune.html: session-owned editing with attachable clients is useful precedent; reject multiplayer and shell-extension scope by default.
- Xi retrospective, https://raphlinus.github.io/xi/2020/06/27/xi-retrospective.html: process-separated frontend/core RPC, pervasive async, CRDTs, and plugin processes consumed excessive novelty and coordination cost. Eon needs a process boundary only when dirty-buffer survival or attachment demonstrably requires it.
- Zed CRDT architecture and DeltaDB, https://zed.dev/blog/crdts and https://zed.dev/blog/introducing-deltadb/: fine-grained concurrent edit and conversation lineage are not unique Eon differentiators. Reject CRDTs and concurrent writers until a real multiplayer requirement exists.
- Agent Client Protocol at pinned Eon reference `9ef3e3800b4070632b54846b5ddf310fc4b35b03`: structured agent communication is preferable to ANSI scraping, but provider sessions remain adapter-owned and distinct from editor documents and Eon work.

## Smallest Observable Decision

Consumer: one local Eon user, with Venus as a transient native client.

Trigger: the user opens or reattaches to one editor surface after the native client was absent.

Candidate result if replacement is earned: one authoritative editor owner supplies a coherent complete semantic document/view snapshot at revision N followed by ordered revisions; accepts semantic modal commands against explicit base revisions; preserves approved Helix-like behavior and keybindings; retains bounded dirty document, selection, and undo state across Venus loss; saves safely; and reports stale edits, external file conflicts, engine loss, incompatible clients, and corrupt recovery state explicitly.

Non-result: this does not promise exact process survival, remote access, cloud sync, multiplayer, CRDT convergence, a plugin system, Helix configuration compatibility, machine-restart recovery, a standalone application, or a supported third-party client. Eon-wide reboot and machine-loss policy remains `eon-decide-eon-session-durability-qhf`.

## Candidate Shapes

1. Keep Helix as an opaque Orbit-hosted child. This remains the default and wins unless dogfood demonstrates a replacement-only contract.
2. Consume a supported upstream Helix semantic or native-client boundary if one exists at decision time. Do not build against an open PR or private fork contract.
3. Reuse selected Helix crates, especially `helix-core`, behind an Eon editor owner while implementing modal command, lifecycle, language, attachment, and Venus projection layers. Apply the dependency and MPL-2.0 license gates to exact files and artifacts.
4. Implement the minimum accepted editor primitives independently, using Helix behavior as a reference corpus. Estimate parity and maintenance honestly.

A full Helix fork, terminal-screen scraping, Neovim-style grid protocol, `helix-view` extraction by assumption, CRDT-first engine, plugin system, cloud service, or distributed process mesh is rejected unless evidence overturns the smaller candidates.

## Ownership Constraints

- The editor engine owns canonical document text, revisions, selections, modal state, transactions, undo, syntax, language integration, safe save, external-change conflicts, and bounded editor recovery state.
- Venus owns native text shaping, drawing, IME, accessibility, pointer input, focus, and ephemeral geometry. It consumes semantic editor projections and never reconstructs document authority from cells or pixels.
- Eon owns workspace topology, product policy, component selection, and references to editor surfaces; it does not implement editing mechanics.
- Orbit retains PTY, process, terminal, history, and terminal-input authority and owns no editor state.
- Provider adapters own provider sessions. Future agents may submit base-revision proposals, but direct agent mutation, isolated worktrees, context manifests, and run provenance remain separately routed through `eon-pxn` and `eon-az9` rather than being prerequisites for the first editor proof.
- Logical ownership does not imply one process per component. Prefer the fewest process and protocol boundaries; require lifecycle evidence before separating the editor engine from the long-lived local workspace host.
- Nice-to-have portability: keep the editor core free of Eon, Orbit, and Venus product types when that does not enlarge the first proof. Eon integration should enter through a narrow adapter, and Venus should be an initial client rather than an engine dependency. This prefers future embedding or a standalone client without promising or building either.

## Prerequisites

- The accepted Helix-based Eon composition remains dogfoodable and supplies concrete limitations caused by the terminal/editor boundary.
- `eon-specify-helix-modal-semantics-3kl` selects the required semantic behavior.
- `eon-preserve-helix-keybindings-uca` selects the binding coverage and workspace-shortcut collision policy.
- The user explicitly activates this decision; deferred status does not make it the active implementation frontier.

## Decision Work

1. Record exact terminal-bound limitations from dogfood and distinguish replacement-only needs from configuration, structured run records, agent worktrees, native review surfaces, or an upstream integration.
2. Reinspect exact current Helix source, relevant upstream client/server work, license, and release/API stability.
3. Compare the four candidate shapes on contract fit, owned and reused LOC, direct/transitive dependencies, language/tooling parity, keybinding and modal fidelity, security, durability, Linux behavior, macOS feasibility, upgrade burden, upstream drift, and removal cost.
4. Produce before-and-after owner and data-flow maps. Select one canonical document owner and the minimum semantic projection; do not create a universal UI or action protocol.
5. Define the smallest falsifiable proof: one document, one client, open/edit/save, approved modal corpus, semantic detach/reattach, bounded dirty-state recovery, stale revision rejection, external-change conflict, and Venus-native input/presentation.
6. Decide whether process separation is necessary. If not, keep the editor owner in the smallest long-lived host; if yes, define start, attach, crash, restart, incompatibility, shutdown, cleanup, queue, and persistence semantics.
7. Obtain an explicit user decision: keep Helix, defer, integrate upstream, reuse selected Helix crates, or authorize an independent engine. Do not implement in this Bead.

## Acceptance

- Exact dogfood evidence identifies at least one valuable contract that requires editor authority, or the decision keeps Helix.
- The keep, upstream integration, selected-crate reuse, and independent-engine shapes are compared at exact revisions with license, dependency, LOC, parity, portability, security, lifecycle, and reversal costs.
- Modal semantics and keybinding continuity decisions are complete and included in every positive cost estimate; reuse of `helix-core` is never treated as automatic behavioral compatibility.
- One owner map covers document text, revisions, selections, modal state, undo, syntax, language services, saves, external changes, workspace references, native projection, terminal state, and provider sessions without duplicate authority.
- The native boundary is semantic, begins with a coherent complete snapshot followed by ordered revisions, and rejects stale or incompatible actions. It is not a terminal grid, raw byte stream, or second handwritten owner schema.
- Persistence is bounded and failure-domain specific. Venus loss may retain dirty editor state; machine restart, cloud sync, remote compute, terminal scrollback, credentials, raw environment, and arbitrary process state remain separate decisions.
- The first proof is one cohesive vertical slice and does not require plugins, CRDTs, multiplayer, remote access, generalized configuration, all Helix UI features, or agent integration.
- The option comparison reports whether the engine core can compile, test, and own documents without importing Eon, Orbit, or Venus product policy. Prefer that direction when it is no larger; record a coupling tradeoff if not. This nice-to-have does not block the Eon-first proof or create a standalone distribution commitment.
- The result records meaningful rejected alternatives, negative evidence, the cheapest proof, the future code-owning repository or explicit owner-selection gate, and an explicit user decision.
- Closure creates no implementation, repository, dependency, protocol, product contract, or Helix removal by itself.

## Verification

- `git -C /home/lucca/pjs/yazelix-dir/helix rev-parse HEAD` must report the inspected revision, or the decision must record and justify a newly inspected exact revision.
- `rg -n "Helix|editor|EON-C4" docs/ARCHITECTURE.md docs/CONTRACTS.md README.md` must confirm the current owner before proposing replacement.
- `br show eon-specify-helix-modal-semantics-3kl --json` and `br show eon-preserve-helix-keybindings-uca --json` must show accepted decisions before a positive recommendation closes.
- The final Bead state must contain reference identities, dogfood evidence, option matrix, owner/data-flow maps, modal/keybinding consequences, proof shape, platform disposition, dependency and license impact, rejected alternatives, and explicit user decision.
- No source, test, manifest, contract index, dependency, generated artifact, ambient configuration, or child repository changes during this decision.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if no replacement-only user value is demonstrated.
- Stop if evidence requires an unapproved dependency, new repository, process boundary, EON/VEN contract, or change to Orbit authority.
- Stop if the proposed engine cannot preserve the accepted Helix modal and keybinding contracts at a credible cost.
- Stop if persistence, agent integration, remote access, CRDTs, plugins, or language parity expand beyond the first falsifiable proof.
- Stop if an upstream API, open PR, license assumption, or unmeasured performance claim is being treated as proven.

## Maintenance Notes

Priority remains P3 and status deferred: this is strategically interesting but not the active product frontier. Effort L for the decision evidence; any editor implementation is XL/HIGH-risk. The most credible positive candidate is selected Helix-core reuse plus Eon-owned modal/lifecycle/projection layers, but that is a hypothesis to test, not a chosen dependency. Helix remains Eon's accepted editor until a separate implementation and acceptance sequence proves and promotes a replacement. Preferred product shape: Eon-first distribution, Eon-independent core when cheap, standalone product deferred.

title: Design and prove the direct Linux release bundle
description:
Contract:
EON-C5.

Prerequisite:
Do not start this bead from completion of the Nix alpha alone. The user must activate distribution graduation through eon-p93 after sustained dogfood.

Goal:
Ship the proven Linux component set as a relocatable archive with an inspectable installation path that does not require Nix. Preserve the accepted Nix component graph and runtime semantics.

Reference and tool gate:
Compare dist, a small owned assembler, and other maintained tools that can consume the canonical manifest. Inspect archive reproducibility, checksums, signatures or attestations, installer generation, rollback, uninstall, multi-architecture support, dependency weight, and local LOC.

Acceptance:
- Publish an immutable archive, checksum, and signature or attestation for each accepted Linux target.
- Support manual extraction plus an installer with dry-run, versioned user prefix, atomic current link, upgrade, rollback, and removal.
- Preserve user data and avoid unrequested shell-profile edits.
- Verify on a clean user environment and record artifact size and closure contents.
- Direct and Nix installations report the same component graph and runtime semantics.
- Prepare yazelix.com installation copy without making the website the binary authority.

Scope:
AppImage, Flatpak, deb, rpm, containers, system repositories, and macOS stay outside this bead.
notes: Reference and tool routing (planning only): Doodlestein Self Releaser is required research evidence beside dist, an owned assembler, Nix-native/local release commands, cost-bounded hosted GitHub Actions, and any other credible shape. Inspect an exact revision for workflow reuse through act, compatibility gaps, artifact naming and parity, verification, upload authority, failure recovery, secrets, signing, and provenance. A local container run does not prove GitHub-hosted parity. Record the expected hosted-minute and storage envelope, timeout and cancellation policy, hard spending boundary, local fallback, and why the selected release owner does not create a second component graph. Reference status does not approve Doodlestein, act, or a workflow.

title: Define the canonical Eon component manifest
description:
Contracts:
EON-C2 and EON-C3.

Goal:
Define one small, human-reviewable manifest that pins exact child revisions, compatibility contracts, and declared package or artifact inputs. Nix consumes this graph during alpha. Later distribution tooling must extend the same graph instead of replacing it.

Reference and tool gate:
Inspect current child release and package metadata plus at least one comparable multi-component manifest. Compare a small hand-owned schema with using existing Nix metadata directly. Record versioning, validation, local LOC, maintenance, and the point at which external release tooling becomes useful. Defer cargo-dist, portable-bundle, and installer evaluation to the direct-distribution gate.

Acceptance:
- The alpha schema names project, revision, contract version, target, package or artifact input, and launch inputs.
- A focused validator rejects incompatible or incomplete component sets.
- One fixture pins the exact owner revisions and contracts required by the alpha: ORB-C1 through ORB-C9, VEN-C1 through VEN-C4, and VEN-C7, their canonical ORBS v2 and ORBF v1 package boundary, plus Helix, Yazi, and Ratconfig. Additional proved contracts may be recorded without becoming activation prerequisites. If preactivation hardening advances an owner proof, pin the final accepted proof rather than preserving an obsolete candidate.
- Eon receives resolved component paths without constructing store paths or invoking a Nix evaluator during normal use.
- Product state records stable component identities instead of resolved store paths.
- docs/CONTRACTS.md records exact proof evidence.

Scope:
Do not require portable artifacts during Nix-only alpha. Do not create a second dependency graph for a package manager or rebuild child behavior in Eon.
close_reason: Strengthened and reverified validation-owner proof with exact public diagnostics for every structured invalid-graph mutation.

User direction after the original gate: the Yazelix stack is Rust-only in general; consider exceptions from first principles, document the reasoning, and continue. Accepted policy for this Bead: durable Eon product behavior and repository tooling are Rust; Nix owns packaging; shell is reserved for irreducible process glue; Python remains suitable only for disposable exploration whose code is not retained. The earlier failing Python-first test is discarded evidence and will be removed before Rust implementation. This is a material code-shape change, so this comment rebaselines the run before Cargo, manifest, test, or generated-lock edits.

Correction to comment 7: its claim that TOML would require another Nix parse path was wrong. Nix provides builtins.fromTOML. JSON is still selected because this artifact is a strict machine-owned dependency graph that needs no comments or TOML-specific types, Nix and Rust both consume it directly, and JSON keeps the persisted surface narrower. The obsolete statement remains in append-only history and is not relied on.

First-principles decision:
- The validator is durable policy: it defines which component graphs Eon accepts. Language consistency therefore affects ownership, review, build reproducibility, onboarding, and removal cost, not just initial LOC.
- Rust gives compile-time schema ownership, one project toolchain, one test/format/lint path, and a reusable library boundary for the later Nix composition without making Nix or shell reinterpret the graph.
- Python would save initial code but introduce a second durable toolchain and split conventions for one small repository. That lifecycle cost exceeds its local brevity here.
- Go would add a second compiled ecosystem with no concurrency, deployment, or service advantage. TypeScript would add Node/package-manager state without a web runtime. Shell/jq would make cross-reference validation less legible. A handwritten JSON parser would avoid crates only by rebuilding a difficult trust boundary.
- Nova at exact commit 124308bfa128203f843839346c88296cd266568a is the local precedent: 47 tracked Rust files, no tracked Python/Go/TypeScript/JavaScript, standard-library Rust utilities compiled directly in flake.nix, and Rust serde_json/toml contract checks. Eon follows the durable-tooling principle, not Nova implementation details.

Crate gate:
- serde 1.0.228 with derive, exact crates.io pin, MIT OR Apache-2.0: owns typed deserialization and unknown-field rejection.
- serde_json 1.0.150, exact crates.io pin, MIT OR Apache-2.0: owns standards-compliant JSON parsing and serialization for mutation tests.
- Normal dependency closure from the already accepted Ratconfig lock and local crate sources is two direct crates plus ten unique transitive crates: serde_core, serde_derive, proc-macro2, quote, syn, unicode-ident, itoa, memchr, and zmij (the direct/unique count includes the shared serde_core only once). All are pure Rust; no native, runtime, Nix service, network, accessibility, input-method, Linux-specific, or macOS-specific behavior is added. The Cargo lock will pin the complete closure. Upgrade burden is one small, conventional parser surface. Replacement cost is deleting the crate and moving the same schema checks to a future accepted owner. Estimated owned Rust is 200–300 lines; serde derive removes more handwritten structural parsing than it adds.
- Rejected: standard-library-only Rust because std has no JSON parser and a local parser would be larger and less correct; jsonschema/schema frameworks because one fixed schema does not justify another dependency/representation; clap/thiserror because std::env, std::error, and Display suffice.

The user approved the Rust direction and continuation after the language comparison. This records that approval for the two exact parser dependencies; it does not approve any runtime, Nix, packaging, release, or child-repository dependency.

title: Prove Home Manager and direct-release parity with Nix Eon
description:
Contract:
EON-C6.

Goal:
Keep the proven Nix package as a supported channel after direct distribution and let Home Manager consume that same package and product contract.

Prerequisites:
- eon-ohh proves the first direct Linux bundle against the same canonical component manifest and accepted runtime semantics.
- The user separately activates Home Manager integration; direct-distribution graduation does not activate another channel automatically.

Reference and tool gate:
Inspect the exact supported Home Manager revision and its official package, module, option, activation, state-version, upgrade, and removal contracts. Compare no Eon-specific integration with `home.packages` consumption and the smallest thin Eon module justified by demonstrated configuration needs. Record Linux target support, evaluation and activation failures, ownership of user files, dependency weight, local LOC, compatibility policy, and removal cost. Reject any shape that creates a Home-Manager-only component graph, settings owner, runtime behavior, or release identity.

Acceptance:
- The original Nix package, Home Manager integration, and direct release consume the same exact component revisions and compatibility metadata.
- Version diagnostics match across channels.
- Runtime behavior and configuration ownership remain channel-independent.
- A clean Nix profile and Home Manager evaluation pass without requiring the direct installer.
- Direct-install users need no Nix evaluator or store.

Scope:
Do not maintain a Home-Manager-only component graph, runtime contract, or feature. This bead does not expand the Nix-only alpha surface.

title: Make Open Eon independent of launcher PATH
description: Harden EON-C1. Consumer: a Linux user invoking the installed Open Eon desktop action. Trigger: the desktop launcher executes the packaged entry with a PATH that does not contain the Nix profile bin directory. Result: the entry invokes the exact installed Eon executable and starts or presents the current generation; live Sessions remain untouched. Failure: package construction must fail if the generated entry cannot be rewritten exactly. Scope: Eon flake desktop packaging, current contract/changelog/LOC, exact artifact build and profile refresh only; no runtime, protocol, child repository, launcher-specific integration, or supervisor restart.
